item.title: From Dot Inc.: Dot Canvas Comes to Android, Expanding Access to Tactile Technology Worldwide
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Dot Canvas is now available on Android, bringing Dot’s tactile technology experience to even more users around the world. Dot Inc. is pleased to announce the release of Dot Canvas for Android, expanding access to Dot Pad and tactile content across a wider range of devices and users. Available through Google Play in 177 countries, … Continue reading From Dot Inc.: Dot Canvas Comes to Android, Expanding Access to Tactile Technology Worldwide
item.content:encoded:
Dot Canvas is now available on Android, bringing Dot’s tactile technology experience to even more users around the world.

Dot Inc. is pleased to announce the release of Dot Canvas for Android, expanding access to Dot Pad and tactile content across a wider range of devices and users.

Available through Google Play in 177 countries, Dot Canvas for Android makes it easier for users to connect with Dot Pad and interact with tactile content using compatible Android devices.

Download Dot Canvas for Android on Google Play

Designed for a global community

Dot Canvas supports 18 languages for the app interface, with the app automatically following the language set on the user’s Android device.

For braille translation, Dot Canvas supports 32 languages, which can be selected directly within the app’s Settings. Support includes languages such as English, Korean, Japanese, Chinese, French, German, Spanish, Arabic, Portuguese, Russian and Welsh.

Selected languages also support both Grade 1 and Grade 2 braille, giving users greater flexibility in how they read and interact with content.

For Simplified Chinese, Dot Canvas also supports three input methods: Xianxing with tone, Xianxing without tone, and Shuang Pin.

Built for Android

Dot Canvas for Android supports devices running Android 8.0 and later, with support across a broad range of Android hardware architectures.

The app is designed for tablets and larger screens, with an 8-inch or larger display and 4GB or more RAM recommended for the best experience. Dot Canvas is designed landscape-first, with landscape use recommended for the most optimized experience.

Dot Pad connects to Android devices via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), supporting one connected Dot Pad at a time.

More ways to access Dot technology

The Android release complements the existing Dot ecosystem, giving users more flexibility in how they access and interact with tactile content.

With Dot Canvas now available across both iOS and Android, Dot continues to make tactile technology more accessible across platforms and around the world.

Get Dot Canvas for Android

This add-on is licensed under the GNU General Public License version 2. The image processing is based on the DotPad prototype add-on created by Michael curran mick@nvaccess.org. Key Commands Image processing details The add-on captures … Continue reading From MAWINGU: Tactile Screen NVDA Add-on
item.content:encoded:
This addon mirrors the computer screen on a DotPad graphical area.

Copyright and License

This add-on is copyright (C) 2026 MAWINGU. This add-on is licensed under the GNU General Public License version 2. The image processing is based on the DotPad prototype add-on created by Michael curran mick@nvaccess.org.

Key Commands

  • control+NVDA+f8: Open connection dialog.
  • NVDA+f8: Displays the screen at the upper left corner of the navigator object, pressed twice will track the navigator object.
  • shift+NvDA+f8: Displays the screen around the mouse pointer, pressed twice will track the mouse pointer.
  • NVDA+Escape: Stops tracking and automatic refresh.

Image processing details

The add-on captures the part of the screen that matches the current zoom level and the coordinates of the navigator object, mouse pointer or the current panned position. The size of the view viewport is a multiple of the graphical area of the connected device. If the image is expected to be black on white, it tries to keep black pixels at the expense of white pixels, and the opposite for white on black. this ensures that thin lines are not removed when shrinking. As the dotpad can only show a monochrome image (I.e. raised dots for white, no dots for black), a suitable threshold must be found to choose how bright something should be to be classed as white. this add-on currently uses a very basic local mean threshold approach where by the average brightness is calculated for a block of 7 by 7 pixels around the pixel in question, and then this value is used as the threshold. this approach ensures that changes can be shown even if lighting changes across the image.

Visit the GitHub repository

item.title: The Global Braille Survey is now open!
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We are delighted to announce that the Global Braille Survey is now open! As part of the Global Braille Literacy Campaign – More Braille: More Empowerment – the survey provides an important opportunity for people around the world to share their experiences and perspectives on braille literacy. Led by the International Council for Education of … Continue reading The Global Braille Survey is now open!
item.content:encoded:
We are delighted to announce that the Global Braille Survey is now open!

As part of the Global Braille Literacy Campaign – More Braille: More Empowerment – the survey provides an important opportunity for people around the world to share their experiences and perspectives on braille literacy.

Led by the International Council for Education of People with Visual Impairment (ICEVI), the World Blind Union (WBU), and collaborating organisations and individuals, this global research initiative aims to strengthen our understanding of how braille is learned, taught, accessed and used – and of the factors that enable or create barriers to braille literacy.

Who can participate?

We warmly invite responses from:

  • Adults aged 18 years and over who are blind, have low vision, or are deafblind;
  • Parents and guardians of children of any age who are blind, have low vision, or are deafblind;
  • Teachers and other professionals involved in braille education; and
  • Braille transcribers.

Share your experience – Take the Global Braille Survey:

tiny.cc/braillesurvey

When you follow the above link, you will first be invited to select your preferred language, then review the informed consent information, and then complete a short set of questions to determine which survey or surveys are relevant to you.

If you are eligible for more than one survey – for example, if you are both an adult braille user and a braille transcriber – you are welcome to contribute from each perspective. Simply complete one survey and then return to the link when you are ready to complete another.

The survey is available in multiple languages

We are delighted that the Global Braille Survey is already available in a growing range of languages, helping to make it possible for more people around the world to participate.

The survey is currently available in Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Hindi, Hungarian, Russian, Slovak, and Spanish.

Italian and Portuguese translations are awaiting verification, and we hope to make these languages available in the near future.

We also warmly welcome offers to assist with translations into additional languages so that the survey can reach an even wider range of countries, communities and language groups. If you have any questions about the survey, or would like to offer assistance with an additional language translation, please contact info@icevi.org.

Why does your participation matter?

Every response adds to our global understanding of braille literacy. The findings will help build a stronger evidence base to inform advocacy, policy, research, resources and practice, and to support efforts to strengthen access to braille literacy around the world.

Please help us spread the word

We want to hear from people across countries, regions, languages and communities.

Please share the Global Braille Survey widely through your organisations, professional and community networks, and directly with braille users, families, educators, professionals and transcribers who may wish to participate.

By sharing the survey widely – including with communities using the languages in which the survey is now available – you can help us hear from as broad and diverse a range of participants as possible.

Every experience matters. Every perspective adds to the evidence. Every voice can help strengthen the future of braille literacy.

Thank you for being part of this important global effort.

item.title: Global Braille Survey Update, 31 August 2026 – More Than 1000 Responses and Growing
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We are delighted to share an encouraging update on the survey, which is a major initiative of the Global Braille Literacy Campaign – More Braille: More Empowerment. More than 1000 surveys have now been completed! This is a wonderful early response. We extend our sincere thanks to everyone who has already participated in the survey … Continue reading Global Braille Survey Update, 31 August 2026 – More Than 1000 Responses and Growing
item.content:encoded:
We are delighted to share an encouraging update on the survey, which is a major initiative of the Global Braille Literacy Campaign – More Braille: More Empowerment.

More than 1000 surveys have now been completed!

This is a wonderful early response. We extend our sincere thanks to everyone who has already participated in the survey and to those who have helped promote it through their organisations, networks and braille communities.

A detailed snapshot taken on 25 August, when 637 surveys had been completed, demonstrates the growing global reach of the initiative:

  • Respondents represented 49 countries and territories.
  • Surveys had been completed in nine languages: English, Spanish, Slovak, German, Russian, French, Hungarian, Simplified Chinese and Hindi.
  • 442 responses (69.4%) were from adults who are blind, have low vision, or are deafblind.
  • 107 responses (16.8%) were from teachers and educational professionals.
  • 74 responses (11.6%) were from braille transcribers.
  • 14 responses (2.2%) were from parents and caregivers.

While we are greatly encouraged by this response, we want to hear from many more people, across many more countries and communities. We particularly welcome your help in reaching braille users, families, educators, professionals and transcribers whose experiences and perspectives may not yet be represented.

Who can participate?

The Global Braille Survey welcomes responses from:

  • Adults aged 18 and over who are blind, have low vision, or are deafblind;
  • Parents and guardians of children of any age who are blind, have low vision, or are deafblind;
  • Teachers and other professionals involved in braille education, including retired professionals who have taught braille; and
  • Braille transcribers.

Take the Global Braille Survey

The survey is currently available in Arabic, Czech, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Hindi, Hungarian, Italian, Nepali Unicode, Portuguese, Russian, Slovak and Spanish.

For people who have difficulty accessing or completing the online survey because of poor internet connectivity, alternative arrangements are available. Please contact info@icevi.org or info@wbu.ngo.

Watch and share the Global Braille Survey launch webinar

The recording of our August 2026 webinar introducing the survey and explaining its purpose is available on YouTube:

You can also share our Instagram post promoting the survey:

We would greatly appreciate your continued support in sharing the survey and webinar recording through your organisations, professional networks and braille communities.

Every response helps us build a stronger global evidence base about how braille is learned, taught, accessed and used, as well as the factors that enable braille literacy or create barriers to it. The findings will help inform future advocacy, policy, research, resources and practice.

Every experience matters. Every perspective adds to the evidence. Every voice can help strengthen the future of braille literacy.

Thank you for helping us build a truly global picture of braille literacy.

item.title: For readers in New Zealand, from Mary Schnackenberg: Single cell macron closer for screen reader users
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The UEB macron is two cells. In New Zealand the macron symbol appears almost exclusively in te reo Māori. When Duxbury worked with us to produce a New Zealand Duxbury template, they agreed to use the single cell macron of dots 456. That was the macron introduced in the mid 1960s. The Māori macron was … Continue reading For readers in New Zealand, from Mary Schnackenberg: Single cell macron closer for screen reader users
item.content:encoded:
The UEB macron is two cells. In New Zealand the macron symbol appears almost exclusively in te reo Māori. When Duxbury worked with us to produce a New Zealand Duxbury template, they agreed to use the single cell macron of dots 456. That was the macron introduced in the mid 1960s. The Māori macron was added to the Duxbury Braille Translator in about 2008.

Some of us with electronic Braille displays have been agitating for some time to get the single cell macron into our screen readers, in particular Jaws and NVDA. At its meeting in June 2026 The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust agreed with and endorsed this effort.

The Braille translator in Jaws and NVDA is Liblouis. Liblouis is one of the Braille translators available in Apple’s iOS.

James Bowden at the RNIB has been updating and correcting the UEB tables for English over several years. He guided Clive Lansink about the creation of Liblouis tables.

Clive has written the New Zealand tables for Liblouis with the one cell macron. The tables are now in the most recent release of Liblouis 3.39.0.

So when will screen reader users be able to choose the new tables? Creators of each of the screen readers have to add new tables manually. I have seen the Liblouis announcement about the latest update. I had absolutely no idea how many changes there are because of so very many languages besides English and te reo Māori. Even so, I have hope we will see the single cell macron in NVDA by this Christmas. I have no idea about Jaws or iOS. If The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust needs to write to screen reader manufacturers, I am sure we will do so.

Thank you so much, Clive, for getting the ball rolling.

item.content:encoded:
For anyone who is interested in trying out what the next version of NVDA has to offer before it is officially released, NV Access welcomes you to download the beta and provide feedback using their issue reporting process.

By installing the beta you will be opting into NVDA’s beta channel, and will only receive update notifications for beta and release candidate (RC) builds.

The beta/RC channel will always keep you up to date with the latest NVDA version.

The last RC in a release cycle is identical to the final stable release.

To return to the stable release channel, upgrade manually to the latest stable build.

Read the full announcement on the NV Access website

We want to understand clearly what is important to you and also identify what we can do more effectively.  This survey is anonymous, and we encourage you to add comments on the survey (but please … Continue reading From NV Access: NVDA Satisfaction Survey 2026
item.content:encoded:
The NVDA Satisfaction Survey 2026 is now open: https://www.nvaccess.org/survey2026

We are always interested in understanding the satisfaction of our NVDA users. We want to understand clearly what is important to you and also identify what we can do more effectively.  This survey is anonymous, and we encourage you to add comments on the survey (but please add your email address if you’d like us to contact you about your feedback).

Last year we had a few questions around “Is your use of NVDA primarily for accessibility testing?” – if you use NVDA to get around the PC, even if you ALSO use it for accessibility testing, you can probably answer “no” to this.  If you are a sighted tester, or primarily use another screen reader and only start NVDA for testing…. then say “yes”.

We’re interested in hearing from as many people as possible, so please feel free to pass this on to others.

OR-bot provides immediate technical guidance for Orbit products, with no registration or login required. It can help you find product-specific technical information, troubleshoot problems, and get answers to commonly asked technical questions. Try OR-bot here. Simply select your Orbit product from the … Continue reading From Orbit Research: Meet OR-bot: Your New Orbit Technical Support Assistant
item.content:encoded:
We are pleased to introduce OR-bot, Orbit Research’s new AI-powered technical support chatbot!

OR-bot provides immediate technical guidance for Orbit products, with no registration or login required. It can help you find product-specific technical information, troubleshoot problems, and get answers to commonly asked technical questions.

Try OR-bot here.

Simply select your Orbit product from the menu and type your question. OR-bot has been designed for screen-reader and keyboard accessibility. It can also respond in multiple languages, although response quality may vary by language.

OR-bot is being introduced as an early release and is still being improved. We invite you to try it with technical questions about the Orbit products you use and share your experience through the Feedback button inside the chatbot. Your feedback will play an important role in helping us make OR-bot better.

OR-bot may occasionally misunderstand a question or provide an incomplete or inaccurate response. If this happens, please try rephrasing your question. OR-bot is an additional support option and does not replace the Orbit Support Team. If you still need technical assistance, please contact us at techsupport@orbitresearch.com.

Please note that conversations may be stored and reviewed to help us improve OR-bot. No personal information is collected, and conversations are not linked to individual users. Please do not include personal or sensitive information in your questions.

We look forward to hearing about your experience with OR-bot.

item.title: From Mathieu via AppleVis: BrailliantConnect: your Brailliant in the Finder, no macFUSE
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: BrailliantConnect is out — free, open source, and finished. Plug a Brailliant in and it appears in the Finder. Unplug it and it goes away. No macFUSE, no kernel extension, nothing to start by hand. I wrote it because I needed it. I use a BI 40X with a screen reader every day, and getting … Continue reading From Mathieu via AppleVis: BrailliantConnect: your Brailliant in the Finder, no macFUSE
item.content:encoded:
BrailliantConnect is out — free, open source, and finished. Plug a Brailliant in and it appears in the Finder. Unplug it and it goes away. No macFUSE, no kernel extension, nothing to start by hand.

I wrote it because I needed it. I use a BI 40X with a screen reader every day, and getting a file onto it from a Mac had stopped being possible in any way I was willing to live with.

What it does

  • The display appears as ~/Brailliant in your home folder.
  • One folder per storage — the display’s own memory, and a USB stick plugged into the display when there is one. Both at once: the stick is no longer invisible.
  • Read and write. Copy files in and out with the Finder, or with anything else that uses the file system.
  • A menu bar item says whether the display is there, and tells you when a copy is still running.

Installing

Unpack, drag into Applications, open it once. That is the whole procedure. It is signed and notarized by Apple, so it opens with no Gatekeeper warning. macOS 11 or later, Intel and Apple Silicon.

One setting, on the display

File transfer (MTP) has to be on. It has been on by default since version 2.5 of the display’s software, so it probably already is. Otherwise: Options, User settings, MTP.

Nothing is switched off by this. Your display publishes its braille interfaces and the file-transfer one at the same time, and stays usable as a braille terminal while files are copying.

What it does not do

  • The Finder returns before a copy is finished. Three gigabytes come back instantly and keep going for about seven minutes. The menu bar says so while it lasts, and notifies you when it lands — do not unplug in between.
  • Changes made on the display itself go unnoticed until the folder is read again. MTP announces nothing.
  • One connection at a time, which only matters if you also use the command-line tool that ships inside the app.

Only one model has been tested

I have a BI 40X, and that is what this was built on. Nothing in the code is tied to a model, but nothing proves the others work either. If you have a BI 20X, a BI 40, or anything else in the family, running brailliant doctor and pasting the output here would settle it — that is the one thing I cannot do alone.

More Info and Download

View the forum post on AppleVis

item.title: From Shahzeb Ahmed: Braille Learn UK
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Hi Braillists Team, I hope you’re well. I’m Shahzeb, a parent of a blind child, and I wanted to share something I created after beginning my own journey of learning Braille alongside my son. When we started, I found it difficult to find a simple and engaging online platform that we could use together. That … Continue reading From Shahzeb Ahmed: Braille Learn UK
item.content:encoded:
Hi Braillists Team,

I hope you’re well.

I’m Shahzeb, a parent of a blind child, and I wanted to share something I created after beginning my own journey of learning Braille alongside my son.

When we started, I found it difficult to find a simple and engaging online platform that we could use together. That experience inspired me to create Braille Learn UK, an online resource with interactive lessons, games and activities to make getting started with Braille a little easier.

I really admire the work the Braillists Foundation does to promote Braille literacy, so I wondered if you would be willing to have a look at the platform.

If you feel it could be useful to your community, I would be incredibly grateful if you might consider sharing it, mentioning it in your newsletter, or including it among your Braille learning resources.

This is a personal project built from my experience as a dad, and ultimately I just want it to reach families and learners who might benefit from it.

Thank you for your time and for everything you do to promote Braille.

Best wishes,
Shahzeb
Braille Learn UK
https://braillelearn.co.uk

item.title: Dr. Cay Holbrook – Remembering a dear colleague and friend
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Posted on behalf of Adam Wilton, Saturday 22 August 2026 Dear colleagues and friends from across Canada and around the world, Our colleague and friend, Dr. Cay Holbrook, reached the end of her journey this morning. Cay passed away peacefully with her family by her side. When Cay entered palliative care a month ago, we … Continue reading Dr. Cay Holbrook – Remembering a dear colleague and friend
item.content:encoded:
Posted on behalf of Adam Wilton, Saturday 22 August 2026

Dear colleagues and friends from across Canada and around the world,

Our colleague and friend, Dr. Cay Holbrook, reached the end of her journey this morning. Cay passed away peacefully with her family by her side. When Cay entered palliative care a month ago, we were not sure how much time we had. This past month has been such a gift, with Cay exuding her characteristic warmth, thoughtfulness, and courage every step of the way.

Over this time, Kim Zebehazy and I have had the great privilege of sharing countless messages of love and support from all over the world. If you sent a message, photo, or a hug along to Cay, please know that she loved and appreciated every single one. We had what we called “dispatches time” at every visit – something we all looked forward to – Cay especially.

A “Celebration of Gratitude” is planned for Tuesday, August 25, 2026 starting at 11:00 AM Pacific time (PDT) at St. David’s United Church in West Vancouver, British Columbia. There is a plan to live stream the celebration via YouTube. The link is posted below:

Dr. Cay Holbrook – Celebration of Gratitude Live Stream, August 25 at 11:00 AM Pacific

There will also be a virtual book of remembrances available via McKenzie Funeral Services. It is not yet up online, but please check back in the days ahead.

Please keep Cay and her family in your thoughts today.

We’ll miss you dearly, Cay, but are renewed in our commitment to everything you stood for, and to carrying forward your legacy in words and deeds. Always in our hearts.

She needs it in braille for her student, and she needs it by tomorrow. If you have been a TVI for any length of … Continue reading From Eye.t: Meet the Eye.t Braille Transcriber, a two-part series: Wednesday 9 and 16 September at 8:00 PM or Thursday 10 and 17 September at 10:30 PM
item.content:encoded:
Introducing

The Eye.t Braille Transcriber

Turn any inaccessible worksheet into formatted braille before your student’s next class

Hi there,

A teacher catches you in the hallway and hands you a worksheet. She needs it in braille for her student, and she needs it by tomorrow. If you have been a TVI for any length of time, you know what that costs you. Transcribing by hand takes hours, and if the page has math or tables on it, longer.

We built the Eye.t Braille Transcriber so you can say yes.

How Does It Work?

A first draft in 60 seconds. Start with a Word document, a PDF, or a photo of a printed page.

Formatting is handled. Headings, lists, and yes, even tables, all formatted to the BANA manual.

Math is recognized automatically. Nemeth or UEB Technical, one click. Spatial math too.

Edit the text or edit the braille. Your choice. Fix the text and the braille updates as you type. Or export to the Braille Editor and enter corrections with six-key entry or a braille display.

The braille matches your student. Build a Student Profile with only the contractions they have learned, and the document comes back partially contracted. Teach a new one, add it, regenerate.

Get a Trial Plus Training!

Reading about it only gets you so far. Meet the Braille Transcriber is two one-hour sessions where you’ll transcribe documents you actually need, alongside us. Bring a worksheet that has been sitting on your desk and leave with it finished.

Both sessions are recorded in case you can’t attend live, and the program carries 2 hours of ACVREP credit. The whole thing is $19. Tuition is free; the $19 covers your 30 day Eye.t Learning Portal license.

Section 1

Wednesday, September 9  ·  3:00 PM ET
Wednesday, September 16  ·  3:00 PM ET

Register for Section 1 →

Section 2

Thursday, September 10  ·  5:30 PM ET
Thursday, September 17  ·  5:30 PM ET

Register for Section 2 →

View Upcoming Cohorts

The Braille Transcriber is included with an Eye.t Instructor license, alongside the rest of the Eye.t Learning Portal. If you’d like to see the whole thing rather than just the braille tool, book a walkthrough and we’ll show you around.

Questions about any of this? Just email info@eyetvision.org and we should get back to you within 24 hours.

Happy teaching!

Cody Laplante

CEO, Eye.t Vision

item.content:encoded:
Imagine entering a ZIP code or postcode and instantly generating a simple, clearly formatted tactile street map that you can explore with your fingers. Pan across the map. Zoom in and out. Find surrounding streets and intersections, and build a mental picture of your neighbourhood, your workplace, your school, or anywhere you’re planning to visit.

That experience is coming to Dot Pad.

Created by accessibility pioneer Dr. Josh Miele, Tactile Map Automated Production (TMAP) has transformed how tactile street maps can be created.

Now, through a collaboration between Josh and Dot Inc., TMAP is coming to Dot Pad — and this webinar is your first opportunity to experience it live!

Register for Navigating the World with TMAP

Join us for a webinar exploring BrailleNote evolve, the next generation Braille computer, and discover what’s new in the latest KeySoft update.

New to BrailleNote evolve? This webinar is for you too. We’ll introduce you to the evolve experience and give you the opportunity to see what makes it different and ask your questions.

Designed to support users from beginner to professional, BrailleNote evolve combines the familiar, accessible experience of KeySoft with the power of a Windows environment and NVDA. It provides a pathway to build confidence and computer literacy while giving experienced users access to the tools they need for education, work and everyday life.

Whether you already own an evolve, are considering one, or simply want to discover what the next generation of Braille computing can offer, we’d love you to join us.

Discover what’s new. Ask questions. Build your skills.

Evolve with us.

item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The sixth generation of the Focus Braille Display is the most powerful and reliable yet, and the new Focus 640 raises the bar for professionals, students, and power users who depend on braille access every day. In this session, Marisa and Ian are joined by special guest Joe McDaniel from Vispero to walk through everything … Continue reading From Access Ingenuity: Focus 640 Braille Display: The Next Generation of High-Performance Braille Access, Wednesday 16 September at 6:00 PM
item.content:encoded:
The sixth generation of the Focus Braille Display is the most powerful and reliable yet, and the new Focus 640 raises the bar for professionals, students, and power users who depend on braille access every day.

In this session, Marisa and Ian are joined by special guest Joe McDaniel from Vispero to walk through everything the Focus 640 brings to the table, from its patented seamless cell cap and redesigned braille pin assembly to its intuitive four-way D-Pad controls and expanded Scratchpad with contracted braille support. Attendees will learn how the Focus 640 connects to multiple Bluetooth devices plus USB-C, delivers extended battery runtime, and works with JAWS for combined speech and braille access including BrailleIn and Braille Study Mode.

The session will also demonstrate something braille users already know and content creators often miss: because a display renders element roles and states directly in the cells, an unlabelled button or a missing form label is immediately visible in braille even when speech output still sounds acceptable. Marisa and Ian will show what well-structured and poorly-structured content each look like on the display, giving attendees a new lens on the documents and websites their organizations produce.

Join Marisa Church and Ian Ramos from Access Ingenuity and Joe McDaniel from Vispero to learn how the Focus 640 delivers exceptional braille performance wherever you need it.

Note that everybody is welcome and can benefit from this presentation. If you are a teacher of the visually impaired (TVI), ACVREP continuing education credit is approved for this presentation.

Join Webinar

Dial By Your Location, Learning Outcomes & Full Webinar Information

item.content:encoded:
Dear friends,

we invite you.

Please share this invitation which you also find here: www.livingbraille.eu/meetup and register yourself in the registration form

Invitation European Braille Meet-Up
4 – 6 December 2026 in Germany (Langenselbold, close to Frankfurt)

Meet with other braille users and experts all over Europe, exchange about braille practice and braille devices and have fun with braille.

Host: European Blind Union (EBU) and German Federation of the Blind and Partially Sighted (DBSV)

Venue: Konferenzhotel Ysenburger Hof
Gelnhäuser Strasse 5, 63505 Langenselbold
www.ysenburgerhof.de
(1 hour by train from Frankfurt airport, 30 minutes from Frankfurt central station; we will try to help you at travelling at the airport and Frankfurt central station; please indicate in the registration form)

Times:

  • Welcome: Friday, 4 December 2026 15:00 CET
  • Official opening: Friday, 4 December 2026 19:30 CET
  • End: 6 December 2026 12:30 CET (followed by lunch)

Language: English

Registration fee including accommodation and meals: 150 €
(The same fee applies to accompanying persons.)

Maximum 90 participants

Please register by 15 November 2026. Accompanying persons, please register separately.
Please use the registration form

You are invited:

  • present practices, methods and devices of learning and using braille in the Show & Tell session.
  • present your knowledge in a “speed presentation” of 15 minutes
  • as producer of braille devices present new products
  • read out braille in your language
  • or simply come along take part

Website: www.livingbraille.eu/meetup

Contact person for questions: Reiner Delgado, r.delgado@dbsv.org

Programme

Friday 4 December

15:00 – 18:00: welcome and braille open space

  • Braille-Art: creating images out of braille patterns
  • Braille Bar I
    participants may ask and discuss any question they might have about the use of braille displays with experts

18:00 – 19:30: dinner

19:30 – 21:00: official opening of Braille Meet-Up

  • greetings/keynote
  • icebreaker games
  • A fun introduction in braille music notation
Saturday, 5 December

9:00 – 10:30: teaching braille

  • tactile training with Punktum, Reiner Delgado (German Federation of the Blind and Partially Sighted)
  • Braille literacy for blind children, Judit Gombas (ELTE Bárczi Gusztáv Faculty of Special Needs Education, Hungary)
  • Teaching braille to adults Ana Gonzalez Arean (Organisación de Ciegos Espanoles)

10:30 – 11:00: coffee break

11:00 – 12:30: multiline and graphic braille displays

  • overview on the current market
  • use cases
  • hands-on experience with devices

Matthew Horspool and Dave Williams (Braillists Foundation, UK), Jesse Wienholts, Netherlands)

12:30 – 13:30: lunch

13:30 – 15:30: Show & Tell
participants are invited to show devices or usecases of teaching and using braille; please indicate n the registration form what you like to present; e.g.

  • your braille display
  • tools for writing braille
  • material and methods for teaching braille
  • creating braille images

15:30 – 16:00: coffee break

16:00 – 17:30: speed presentations I (15 minutes each)
please indicate on the registration form, if you want to present something

  • what Unified English Braille means (Matthew Horspool)
  • tactile lettering – why do we need standards like EN18156  (Bart Simons, Dutsh Braille Authority))
  • What is the new E-Braille format?, James Bowden (RNIB, UK)

17:30 – 18:30: Braille Bar II
participants may ask and discuss any question they might have about the use of braille displays with experts

18:30 – 20:00: dinner

20:15 – 21:30: cultural event
reading out from braille the fairytale Ciderella in different languages
Please indicate in the registration form, if you want to read.

Sunday, 6 December

9:00 – 10:30: speed presentations II (15 minutes each)
please indicate on the registration form, if you want to present something

10:30 – 11:00: coffee break

11:00 – 12:30: Br-AI-lle – what’s going on with braille and artificial intelligence?
How AI can improve braille currently and in the future
Oleg Shevkun (Germany)

13:00: lunch

item.title: For Readers in New Zealand: Do Braille standards matter to you, now and into the future?
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust (BANZAT) has vacancies for three trustees. The closing date for expressions of interest is Monday 14 September 2026. BANZAT sets standards and makes rulings on Braille code and format usage within New Zealand, maintaining consistency with Rules and Guidelines set by the International Council on English Braille. … Continue reading For Readers in New Zealand: Do Braille standards matter to you, now and into the future?
item.content:encoded:
The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust (BANZAT) has vacancies for three trustees. The closing date for expressions of interest is Monday 14 September 2026.

BANZAT sets standards and makes rulings on Braille code and format usage within New Zealand, maintaining consistency with Rules and Guidelines set by the International Council on English Braille. Trustees uphold the agreement with Kāpō Māori Aotearoa about rules for transcribing te reo Māori into Braille. BANZAT also accredits practitioners involved in Braille production. Trustees monitor the adherence of all Braille producers to the standards set by the Trust and, where appropriate, draws attention to breaches of standards in quality or accuracy of Braille produced within New Zealand. The Trust promotes Braille as the prime literacy medium for blind people.

The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust welcomes expressions of interest from anyone in New Zealand who would be willing to serve as a BANZAT Trustee. Your three-year term begins on 25 November 2026 at the conclusion of the Trust’s Annual General Meeting and will conclude at the AGM in 2029. Trustees are eligible for reappointment.

Applicants should demonstrate knowledge, experience or lived experience relating to the Braille community. All trustees must be able to read uncontracted Braille by touch or sight, and the Trust seeks to maintain a balanced mix of advanced Braille expertise, recognised qualifications, technical knowledge, teaching or transcription experience, and an understanding of and respect for current Braille standards and practice.

For details of the qualifications and experience necessary for trustees please refer to section 3.3 of the BANZAT Trust Deed.

You can find out more about the Trust from this website, https://www.banzat.org.nz/.

The closing date for expressions of interest is Monday 14 September 2026. Trustees plan to make their selection by the end of September in time for the successful candidates to attend the Annual General Meeting of BANZAT on Wednesday 25 November 2026.

For further inquiries or to send your expression of interest please contact the Secretary of The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust:
Mary Schnackenberg
Email Secretary@banzat.org.nz

Application Deadline: October 1, 2026 We would be very grateful for your help in sharing this opportunity widely with blind and visually … Continue reading Applications Now Open – 2026 BMF International Music Competition for the Blind, Deadline Thursday 1 October
item.content:encoded:
Dear Musicians, Educators, and Colleagues,

Greetings from Bella Music Foundation!

We are pleased to announce that applications are now open for the 2026 BMF International Music Competition for Blind and Visually Impaired Musicians.

Application Deadline: October 1, 2026

We would be very grateful for your help in sharing this opportunity widely with blind and visually impaired student musicians, young artists, music teachers, schools, universities, and organizations in your network. We hope to reach as many talented blind and visually impaired musicians as possible and encourage them to take advantage of this international performance and career-development opportunity.

The competition welcomes blind and visually impaired classical and jazz musicians from around the world and provides opportunities to showcase their artistry, receive recognition, and advance their musical careers.

Competition Highlights

USD 10,000 in Total Cash Awards

Carnegie Hall Performance Opportunity – All First Prize winners will be invited to perform at the Finale Concert of the 2026 BMF National Concert Tour Series on December 6, 2026, at Carnegie Hall – Weill Recital Hall in New York City

Additional First Prize Awards Sponsored by Dancing Dots – Each First Prize winner will receive either the GoodFeel suite (valued at $1,895) or Lime Lighter Liberty (valued at $1,849), depending on the winner’s individual needs

Eligibility

Open to blind and visually impaired instrumentalists, vocalists, and composers of any nationality.

Classical: Ages 10–30

Jazz: Ages 15–30

Audition Process

Preliminary Round: Recorded Video Audition
Application & Submission Deadline: October 1, 2026

Final Round: Live Zoom Audition, October 15–19, 2026

For complete competition regulations and application information, please visit our website: https://www.bellamf.org/bmf-intl-music-competition/2026-bella-music-foundation-international-music-competition-for-the-blind-and-visually-impaired-musicians

Please help us spread the word and encourage eligible blind and visually impaired students and musicians to apply before the October 1 deadline. Your support in sharing this opportunity with your community would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you for helping us reach and support talented blind and visually impaired musicians around the world.

item.title: UN Committee on Rights of Persons with Disabilities supports ICEVI – WBU Global Declaration on Braille Literacy
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: From the WBU: I am pleased to announce that the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), an 18 member Committee of experts, issued a statement in support of the ICEVI – WBU Global Declaration on Braille Literacy at the closing of its 35th session held from August 12 – 27, 2026 … Continue reading UN Committee on Rights of Persons with Disabilities supports ICEVI – WBU Global Declaration on Braille Literacy
item.content:encoded:
From the WBU:

I am pleased to announce that the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), an 18 member Committee of experts, issued a statement in support of the ICEVI – WBU Global Declaration on Braille Literacy at the closing of its 35th session held from August 12 – 27, 2026 in Geneva, Switzerland.

The Committee welcomed the Global Declaration on Braille Literacy, holding that it is “a significant initiative of organizations of persons with disabilities and civil society organizations to strengthen implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.”  The Committee further stated that ““By reaffirming braille literacy as both a human rights obligation and a strategic investment in national development, the Declaration provides States Parties with an evidence-informed framework for advancing the educational achievement, independence, and full participation of persons who are blind, deafblind or partially sighted in accordance with the Convention.”

Full Statement

Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities

35th session (12-27 August)

Geneva, 27 August 2026

Braille Literacy in Education: Implementing the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities

The Committee welcomes the Global Declaration on Braille Literacy in Education, jointly issued by the World Blind Union (WBU) and the International Council for Education of People with Visual Impairment (ICEVI), a significant initiative of organizations of persons with disabilities and civil society organizations to strengthen implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

The Committee notes that the Declaration clarifies how existing obligations under the Convention should be implemented to ensure equitable access to braille literacy.

The Committee considers that the Declaration is grounded in the Convention, and is particularly related to Articles 9 (Accessibility), 21 (Freedom of Expression and Opinion, and Access to Information), 19 (Living independently and being included in the community), 21 (Freedom of expression and opinion, and access to information), and 24 (Education), and 30 (Participation in cultural life, recreation, leisure and sport). Together, these provisions require that persons who are blind, deafblind or partially sighted have access to information and education through appropriate modes of communication, including braille. The Declaration therefore presents braille literacy not as a specialised educational service, but as a fundamental means through which States Parties fulfil their obligations under the Convention.

The Declaration highlights the strong relationship between braille literacy and improved educational attainment, employment, economic participation, and independent living. Available research and evidence demonstrate that investment in braille instruction delivers measurable social and economic returns while advancing equality, inclusion, and full participation. The Declaration also addresses the misconception that digital technology has diminished the importance of braille. Instead, it recognises that accessible digital technologies and braille are complementary and mutually reinforcing. Screen readers synthetic speech, and audiobooks expand access to information but do not replace the literacy competencies developed through reading and writing braille. Digital technologies, including braille note-takers, refreshable braille displays and dedicated braille practice applications, facilitate braille access, use, learning and literacy. Together, braille and accessible technology provide the strongest foundation for educational achievement and lifelong participation. To that end the Committee highlights the need to ensure interoperability between accessible and assistive technologies.

To strengthen implementation of Article 24, the Declaration calls on States Parties to incorporate braille literacy into national legislation and education policy, ensure timely assessment of learners’ requirements, provide qualified specialist teachers and accessible learning materials, guarantee equitable access regardless of geography or resources, and sustain long-term investment in braille education systems. These recommendations align closely with the Convention’s principles and obligations of accessibility, inclusive education, equality of opportunity, and international cooperation.

The Committee welcomes that Declaration has received broad international endorsement from organisations of persons with visual impairment, educational institutions, professionals, researchers, and advocates. This support reflects a growing global consensus that braille literacy remains essential to achieving inclusive and equitable education.

By reaffirming braille literacy as both a human rights obligation and a strategic investment in national development, the Declaration provides States Parties with an evidence-informed framework for advancing the educational achievement, independence, and full participation of persons who are blind, deafblind or partially sighted in accordance with the Convention.

The Committee calls upon United Nations concerned departments and units to continue providing documents in Braille, pursuant to their duties under the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, so that persons with disabilities who are blind can have ongoing access to information and updates.

item.content:encoded:
When many people think about public uses of braille, they picture those bumpy dots on bathroom door signs or below elevator buttons. The Lafayette-based company, Tactile Engineering, created a new public display of braille in use. This past May, blind race fans were able to enjoy the Indianapolis 500 via the Cadence Tactile Tablet, which allowed them to feel the movement of the cars beneath their fingers in real time.

item.title: Donate to the Braillists by Joining a UK-Based Research Panel
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We have been approached by Contact Design and Survey Feeds, a market research agency, who are looking for UK-based blind and partially sighted people to join their database to be contacted about paid research studies from the financial industry. they are offering a sign-up bonus of $100 USD (£74.79) to everyone who is approved for … Continue reading Donate to the Braillists by Joining a UK-Based Research Panel
item.content:encoded:
We have been approached by Contact Design and Survey Feeds, a market research agency, who are looking for UK-based blind and partially sighted people to join their database to be contacted about paid research studies from the financial industry.

they are offering a sign-up bonus of $100 USD (£74.79) to everyone who is approved for the panel, with additional payments when you participate in a study.

They will also donate $100 USD (£74.79) to the Braillists for everyone who is approved for the panel who signs up via our unique link.

Further information can be found below.

Use our unique link to take the screener survey and join the panel

Contact Design says:

This accessibility panel is designed to help us better understand how people with diverse accessibility needs navigate digital platforms — so we can make them more usable, inclusive, and enjoyable for everyone.

This panel is managed by IPSOS, who will periodically reach out with opportunities to participate in upcoming research. All participation is completely voluntary, and opportunities vary depending on your availability and interests.

What You May Be Invited To Do

  • Short online surveys — sometimes individually compensated, sometimes entered into a prize or raffle.
  • Remote or in person interviews (60–90 minutes) — where you’ll interact with websites, apps, or features and share your feedback.
  • Usability sessions — hands on activities to help improve accessibility and user experience.
  • Availability checks — for longer studies, you may receive a quick call or text.
  • Email only invitations — for short surveys and simple studies.

Welcome Gift

Once approved, you’ll receive a $100 USD (74.79 GBP) welcome gift via PayPal

How to Join

If you’re interested in joining, please complete the screening survey.

It takes about 15 minutes.

We ask detailed questions now so you won’t have to answer them repeatedly later. This helps us match you with studies that fit your profile and accessibility needs.

Next Steps

If you qualify, we will contact you by phone to confirm your participation.

Referral Program

We’re continuing to grow this panel and are especially looking for individuals with similar accessibility needs.

  • Earn $25 USD (18.70 GBP) per approved referral
  • Share out your referral link (you can get this from the person who recruits you for the panel).

We look forward to hearing from you! Thanks!

Use our unique link to take the screener survey and join the panel

item.title: MORE BRAILLE: MORE EMPOWERMENT – Launching the Global Braille Survey, Friday 7 August at 12:00 PM or Tuesday 11 August at 1:00 AM
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: When we talk about braille, we often hear statements like: But how true are they? Help us on our mission to find out! A global braille survey is being launched by the International Council for Education of People with Vision Impairment (ICEVI) and the World Blind Union through their braille literacy campaign More Braille: More … Continue reading MORE BRAILLE: MORE EMPOWERMENT – Launching the Global Braille Survey, Friday 7 August at 12:00 PM or Tuesday 11 August at 1:00 AM
item.content:encoded:
When we talk about braille, we often hear statements like:

  • “Only 7–10% of blind people read braille.”
  • “Blind children aren’t learning braille at school like they used to.”
  • “Technology is making braille irrelevant.”

But how true are they?

Help us on our mission to find out!

A global braille survey is being launched by the International Council for Education of People with Vision Impairment (ICEVI) and the World Blind Union through their braille literacy campaign More Braille: More Empowerment. The survey is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to build a comprehensive understanding of the international braille landscape, ensuring that future braille initiatives are informed by evidence, respond to real needs, and help secure future investment in braille literacy.

Join us for this special event to find out:

  • Why do we need a survey like this?
  • What will happen to the data?
  • Who can take the survey?
  • How long will it take to complete?
  • Will it be available in multiple languages?
  • When will it close?

Hear first-hand from senior leaders in ICEVI and WBU, members of the Global Braille Literacy Campaign Steering Committee and the researchers who compiled the survey, and discover how organisations are already planning to incorporate the results of the survey into their future work.

There will be time for questions at the end of the event.

Let your story shape braille’s next chapter. We look forward to your company!

Register for Launching the Global Braille Survey

To join by phone, please use these details:

  • Meeting ID: 856 5952 0002
  • Passcode: 123456

item.title: From the Standards and Testing Agency: Notification of Modified Tests Framework 2027-2031 Pre-Market Engagement Event, Monday 17 August at 2:00 PM
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The Standards and Testing Agency (STA), an Executive Agency of the Department for Education (DfE), is looking to re-establish a Modified Tests Framework for the development and delivery of modified versions of National Curriculum Tests for children with visual impairments, hearing impairments and special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The new framework will be for … Continue reading From the Standards and Testing Agency: Notification of Modified Tests Framework 2027-2031 Pre-Market Engagement Event, Monday 17 August at 2:00 PM
item.content:encoded:
The Standards and Testing Agency (STA), an Executive Agency of the Department for Education (DfE), is looking to re-establish a Modified Tests Framework for the development and delivery of modified versions of National Curriculum Tests for children with visual impairments, hearing impairments and special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The new framework will be for four years from 1 February 2027 to 31 January 2031.

Successful suppliers will be required to provide modified versions of standard tests in various formats including modified large print and Unified English Braille. Modified versions are required for all national curriculum tests including the following:

  • Phonics Screening Check (braille version only);
  • Key stage 1 tests in English Grammar Punctuation and Spelling, English Reading, Mathematics and;
  • Key stage 2 tests in English Grammar Punctuation and Spelling, English Reading, Mathematics and;
  • Key stage 3 English Reading.

However, this is subject to change depending on government policy.  The tests required for modification will be specified in each call-off.

Suppliers will also be expected to provide:

  • assessment reports evaluating suitability of test items including recommendations for modifications for future test development.
  • amendments to the standard mark scheme guidance to enable consistent marking of the modified versions of the Live tests;
  • braille proofing and quality assurance of Grade 1 and 2 UEB versions of the national curriculum tests;
  • a specialist helpline service:
  • to answer queries from schools and other users of modified tests;
  • to facilitate on-demand orders of past test Braille materials and the replacements of reception baselines assessment resources
  • to validate Modified test orders for the incumbent Test Operations Supplier
  • to facilitate late Modified test orders for the incumbent Test Operations Supplier

The market engagement event will be held virtually via Microsoft Teams on 17 August 2026 between 2 – 4PM BST.  To participate, potential bidders must register on Jaggaer (or access their existing account) and express an interest in ssq_830. Once an expression of interest has been submitted, further information will be provided, including joining instructions for the event. Suppliers will also have the opportunity to ask questions relating to the event and the subsequent procurement.

Jaggaer Registration Link: https://education.app.jaggaer.com/web/login.html The Prior Information Notice (PIN) in relation to this pre-market engagement can be found at: Modified Test Framework 2027/2031 Market Engagement Event – Find a Tender

item.title: From Sertec: Braille Festival, thursday 5-Saturday 7 November, Portugal
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Sertec is organizing a major event to bring civil society together around the braille system in its many forms. We want to show how this unique system of reading and writing is the gateway that opens the world to all blind people, and how we all benefit from getting to know it better. The event … Continue reading From Sertec: Braille Festival, thursday 5-Saturday 7 November, Portugal
item.content:encoded:
Sertec is organizing a major event to bring civil society together around the braille system in its many forms.

We want to show how this unique system of reading and writing is the gateway that opens the world to all blind people, and how we all benefit from getting to know it better.

The event will last 3 days, with the first two days taking place exclusively online and the final day in person.

  • Dates: November 5-7, 2026
  • Location (November 7): Maria Amália Vaz de Carvalho Secondary School, Lisbon

Online Sessions

The online sessions will take place throughout the day, last 60 minutes each, and cover topics as diverse as early childhood, braille scripts, assistive technologies, and international research in the field of braille.

In-Person Day

A true day of celebration, featuring themed exhibits, an Assistive Technology Fair, workshops, board games, and sports. There will be a space for rest and refreshments, and we haven’t forgotten our four-legged friends. The day will conclude with a closing show.

Call for Participation

  • Would you like to suggest a topic?
  • Do you have expertise in a specific area that you’d like to share at the Festival?
  • Would you like to perform in the closing show?
  • Would you like to help out as a volunteer?
  • Is your organization interested in having a booth or leading an activity?

Get in touch with us.

A dedicated website for the event will be launched shortly. Until then, those interested in participating can send an email to festivaldobraille@sertec.pt expressing their interest to be added to the mailing list for festival updates.

July 25 marked one year since the Learning and Use of Braille was designated as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Portugal. This important recognition, combined with the celebration of the 200th anniversary of the invention of the braille system, makes this a particularly significant moment for holding the Braille Festival.

We will make every effort to bring together people from all walks of life for this event: users, teachers, businesspeople, cultural and sports leaders … We want to convey the idea that braille is for everyone, and that in an inclusive society, it brings people together, fosters growth, and helps eliminate prejudices and barriers.

Braille is magical, fun, and powerful … it cannot be confined to a niche in society.

We’re counting on you!

How can you reach us?

You can contact us by phone at 219435183 or 930553007.

Our email is info@sertec.pt

The new Sertec is located at the top of Alameda Afonso Henriques, right behind the Fonte Luminosa fountain.

The nearest Metro station is Alameda, 400 meters away.

Buses: 208, 720, 730, 756, 793

Parking: There are a few parking spaces in front of the store, but you’ll find it easier to park on Alameda Afonso Henriques or on Rua Cristóvão Falcão if you’re coming from the Rotunda das Olaias. There’s also an EMEL parking lot next to the António Arroio School.

GPS: 38.737427 N, -9.128911 W

Rua Barão de Sabrosa, 165-B

item.title: From Judith Lung: DottedNotes — Bidirectional Braille ⇄ LilyPond/MusicXML Translator
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: (Built out of my own frustration transcribing orchestral scores) Contact: judith@judithlung.com I’m a blind composer, and for years my biggest bottleneck wasn’t writing the music — it was getting it out of braille and into something a publisher, ensemble, or sighted collaborator could actually use. Transcribing an orchestral score from braille into LilyPond by hand … Continue reading From Judith Lung: DottedNotes — Bidirectional Braille ⇄ LilyPond/MusicXML Translator
item.content:encoded:
(Built out of my own frustration transcribing orchestral scores)

Contact: judith@judithlung.com

I’m a blind composer, and for years my biggest bottleneck wasn’t writing the music — it was getting it out of braille and into something a publisher, ensemble, or sighted collaborator could actually use.

Transcribing an orchestral score from braille into LilyPond by hand could eat several days of work before I’d even gotten to the actual engraving and proofing. That grind is what pushed me to build DottedNotes.

It’s a free, bidirectional translator between:

  • Braille music (.brf / .brl)
  • LilyPond (.ly, which compiles straight to publication-quality .pdf and .midi)
  • MusicXML (.musicxml / .mxl)

So you can go from a braille manuscript to a publisher-ready PDF and MIDI in one pass, or take a print/MusicXML score and export a proper braille edition — with BANA validation built in (standard or strict profile), configurable compression levels, and layout presets for solo piano, art song, chamber, orchestral, and lead sheet scores, since orchestral formatting has its own headaches that a generic converter won’t get right.

It’s also useful if you’re a sighted composer, engraver, or publisher who needs to move a score between these formats, or produce a braille edition without knowing braille music code yourself.

Free to use here: https://www.dottednotes.net/

I built this to solve my own problem, but I know braille music workflows vary a lot person to person, so I’d genuinely appreciate feedback from other blind musicians — especially anyone who’s dealt with the same orchestral-score transcription slog. Bug reports, edge cases in the braille code handling, feature requests all welcome.

item.title: From TifloAcosta: Braillito, a fun way to discover Braille
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Braillito is an app designed to bring braille closer to anyone who wants to learn it in a simple and enjoyable way. It is aimed at blind people who are beginning to explore braille, but also at family members, teachers, students, and anyone curious about how braille works. The app offers a progressive learning experience … Continue reading From TifloAcosta: Braillito, a fun way to discover Braille
item.content:encoded:
Braillito is an app designed to bring braille closer to anyone who wants to learn it in a simple and enjoyable way.

It is aimed at blind people who are beginning to explore braille, but also at family members, teachers, students, and anyone curious about how braille works.

The app offers a progressive learning experience through lessons, exercises, and small games. Users can practice letters, numbers, and symbols, build words, explore braille equivalents, and gradually track their progress.

What I like most is its educational value. Anything that helps make braille better known, more approachable, and less like a mysterious code reserved for a few people is always welcome.

That said, it is important to remember one thing. Learning the braille code is only part of the journey. Braille also requires real hands-on practice. In the end, your fingers have to do their job because, as useful as apps may be, they still cannot read braille over Bluetooth.

For that reason, I see Braillito as a great starting point, an enjoyable way to begin learning, and a useful companion for anyone who later wants to continue with real braille materials.

Download

Download from the App Store

Download from Google Play
