item.title: From the Braille Authority of North America: BANA Publishes Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics and Science in UEB
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Press Release July 2026 For Immediate Release Contact: Jen Goulden, BANA ChairBraille Authority of North America613-552-4191chair@brailleauthority.org At its face-to-face meeting in May, the Braille Authority of North America (BANA) approved Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics and Science in UEB. This publication replaces Provisional Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics in UEB and is now available in PDF and BRF versions on the … Continue reading From the Braille Authority of North America: BANA Publishes Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics and Science in UEB
item.content:encoded:
Press Release

July 2026

For Immediate Release

Contact: Jen Goulden, BANA Chair
Braille Authority of North America
613-552-4191
chair@brailleauthority.org

At its face-to-face meeting in May, the Braille Authority of North America (BANA) approved Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics and Science in UEB. This publication replaces Provisional Guidance on Transcribing Mathematics in UEB and is now available in PDF and BRF versions on the BANA website. A direct link to that page is https://www.brailleauthority.org/unified-english-braille-codebooks.

The newly adopted guidance document incorporates recent revisions to the international publication Guidelines for Technical Material, section 1.7 Choice and Placement of Grade 1 Indicators, by the International Council on English Braille (ICEB). The guidance document also includes an expanded selection of examples to illustrate transcription of math and science expressions in UEB.

The mission of the Braille Authority of North America is to assure literacy for tactile readers through the standardization of braille and/or tactile graphics.

You can follow the work of BANA through Facebook and X and BANA’s website at https://www.brailleauthority.org/

item.title: From the Braille Revival League of Texas: Recommended Changes to the Texas Education Code to Enhance Braille Literacy for Students (K-12)
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: BRAILLE IS LITERACY Access to higher education, career training programs, and employment opportunities for blind and low vision students depend upon literacy, and braille is the key to literacy and independence for people who are blind or have low vision. The total number of students reported in the Annual Registration of Students with Low Vision … Continue reading From the Braille Revival League of Texas: Recommended Changes to the Texas Education Code to Enhance Braille Literacy for Students (K-12)
item.content:encoded:
BRAILLE IS LITERACY

Access to higher education, career training programs, and employment opportunities for blind and low vision students depend upon literacy, and braille is the key to literacy and independence for people who are blind or have low vision.

The total number of students reported in the Annual Registration of Students with Low Vision in Texas this year is 10,853. Shockingly, only 732 of these students (just 6.7%) use braille as a reading medium, and less than half of them use it as their primary reading medium.

The Texas Governor’s Committee on People with Disabilities recently completed and distributed a report recommending seven important changes to the Texas Education Agency code which would result in enhancing the availability, teaching and use of braille study and test materials for blind and low vision students and their teachers.

The Braille Revival League of Texas fully supports these recommendations and urges their adoption by the Texas State Legislature.

Recommendation 1: Amend Chapter 30, Education Code Sec. 30.002(c) and related statutes by requiring a unanimous decision by the ARD committee before braille can be determined to be a medium that is not appropriate for a student who is blind, deafblind, or has low vision.

Recommendation 9: Amend Section 30.002(c) to clarify that literacy includes math literacy skills, and that braille must be used across educational contexts.

Recommendation 13: Amend Chapter 30 Education Code Sec. 30.002(b) by adding (4) provide access to braille instructional materials and embossed braille statewide testing materials at no cost to districts if print or electronic copies are provided at no cost.

Recommendation 14: Amend Chapter 31 Education Code Sec. 31.028(a) to add the requirement that the commissioner ensures students with visual impairments have access to their instructional materials at the same time as, or earlier than, their peers have access to their non-adapted materials. This must be supported by the creation of a centralized service in Texas offering braille transcription and tactile graphics produced when requested.

Recommendation 15: Amend Chapter 31 Education Code Sec. 31.028(a) to add a requirement that TSVIs, who need an adapted teacher edition (braille or large print), will receive their adapted teacher edition at the same time that other teachers receive their non-adapted teacher edition.

Recommendation 17: Amend Chapter 30 Education Code Sec. 30.002(c)(6) to add year-round (B) access to their assistive technology and instructional materials.

Recommendation 21: Amend Chapter 30 Education Code Sec. 30.002(c)(7) to include a requirement for TSVIs to receive at least 6 hours of professional development training in braille every five years.

item.title: From Orbit Research: Software Version 2.1 is now available for Orbit Speak
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Greetings from Orbit Research! We are pleased to announce the availability of a long awaited, new software update, version 2.1, for the Orbit Speak and Orbit Speak Plus notetakers. This is a major new release, bringing Orbit Speak to our version 2.x platform, aligning it with all the latest features available on our orbit Player, … Continue reading From Orbit Research: Software Version 2.1 is now available for Orbit Speak
item.content:encoded:
Greetings from Orbit Research!

We are pleased to announce the availability of a long awaited, new software update, version 2.1, for the Orbit Speak and Orbit Speak Plus notetakers.

This is a major new release, bringing Orbit Speak to our version 2.x platform, aligning it with all the latest features available on our orbit Player, as well as introducing system-wide Braille translation support.

The update can be installed by using the automatic software update feature built into the Orbit Speak. Instructions on performing this process are provided below.

Important notes

  • Installing this release requires 2 steps – first, installing a special build of version 1.x that will allow upgrading to 2.1, and then performing the actual upgrade. Please carefully read all the info provided in the installation steps section.
  • After upgrading to version 2.1, due to major differences between the 2 platforms, data store in our applications such as bookmarks in books, subscribed podcasts, etc, will have to be re-added. Physical data copied to the device, such as music, books, etc, will stay in place.
  • Support for 3rd party Android applications, which for now includes NLS Bard, will be rolled out a bit later.
  • Some functionality has been moved, changed or refined in the 2.1 software compared to 1.x applications. Please consult the updated user guide for changes.
  • There is now a new Braille settings section, under the device settings option, that allows selecting the Braille table used for input, as well as the preferred Braille grade. Once configured, you can switch between the selected Braille grades for the chosen language with space + g )dots 1-2-4-5(. This will cycle between the tables chosen for Computer Braille, contracted, and uncontracted Braille.
  • The update also includes a firmware upgrade. Please be patient when performing the update process for it to fully complete.

New features

Here is a short list of the new features available with this major update. Please consult the updated user guide for more details:

  1. System-wide Braille translation, including on the fly switching between Braille grades.
  2. Internet radio: import/export.
  3. Improved editor with enhanced Say All capabilities, including better cursor tracking.
  4. New world clock, stopwatch, and countdown timer apps.
  5. A new screen reader with better announcement of system prompts, as well as a more responsive overall look and feel.
  6. Re-organized home screen for easier location of important features.
  7. A Braille reader application on orbit Speak Plus for easier reading of BRF files including bookmarks, etc, linked to our book reader.
  8. New software architecture that enables easier updates and quicker bug fixing on an individual application level.
  9. A completely re-designed media player, with proper music library management / playlist capabilities.

Steps for updating the software

Please follow the steps below to update the software. If you have already set up your Wi-Fi connection, you will automatically be notified of new software updates and will be able to download and install them easily.

Here are the steps to connect to a Wi-Fi network, if you have not already done so:

  1. From the home menu, locate the settings item and activate it with dot 8 or the select key. You can also press the letter s to enter settings directly.
  2. In the settings application, locate the Wi-Fi settings item and activate it with dot 8 or select. You can also press w to enter it directly.
  3. The device will scan for available networks and will show the network list. Locate your network and press the dot 8 or select key.
  4. A menu will pop up with an option to connect to the network. Activate this option with dot 8 or select.
  5. If the network is password protected, a dialog will pop up asking you to enter the password. Please enter the password in computer braille and press dot 8.
  6. The device will connect to the network and give you an indication that the connection has been successfully completed.
  7. You can now press space + dots 1-2-3-4-5-6 to go back to the home menu.

Once your Orbit Speak is connected to the Wi-Fi network, the following are the steps for updating the software:

Step 1: Installing the transition build
  1. From the main menu, navigate to the settings item and activate it with dot 8 or select.
  2. Locate the “software update” item inside of the settings list and activate it with dot 8 or select. You can also press the letter u to enter it directly.
  3. Locate the check for updates now button and press dot 8 or select to activate it.
  4. The device will tell you that there is a newer software version available and will ask you if you want to install it. Activate the yes button inside the dialog that will pop up. The version you’ll be offered is 1.9.0.1.
  5. Wait until the device downloads, installs the update, and restarts. Progress indications will be given throughout the process.
Step 2: upgrading to 2.1

Once the transition build is installed, follow these steps to upgrade to the actual 2.1 software:

  1. From the home screen, find and activate the Utilities menu.
    1. Inside of the Utilities menu, find and activate the newly added “Upgrade to Orbit Speak 2.0” option.
    1. When prompted if you wish to upgrade, activate the yes button and wait until the device restarts.
    1. Once the device restarts, you will hear Orbit Speak announce the home screen.
    1. Note: the first startup can take longer than usual.

item.title: From Blazie Technologies: August 2026 BT Speak and BT Braille Release Notes
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Introduction Blazie Technologies is excited to introduce the August update for BT Speak and BT Braille. It features the first phase of our work to greatly enhance Braille quality and accuracy across both products. In particular, the update brings substantial improvements to English literary Braille accuracy and input feedback, plus a new comprehensive Braille help … Continue reading From Blazie Technologies: August 2026 BT Speak and BT Braille Release Notes
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Blazie Technologies is excited to introduce the August update for BT Speak and BT Braille. It features the first phase of our work to greatly enhance Braille quality and accuracy across both products. In particular, the update brings substantial improvements to English literary Braille accuracy and input feedback, plus a new comprehensive Braille help topic. The Editor now lets you keep task lists with to-do items in your documents. New links in the Editor can open web pages, headings and other files, making documents easier to organize and navigate. DECtalk speech, media, NFB Newsline, device performance and reliability have also been improved.

Quick Instructions for Updating Your BT Speak or BT Braille

  1. Ensure that your BlazieTech device is connected to a Wi-Fi network. The battery level should be 40% or higher.
  2. Type O-Chord for the Options menu.
  3. Type M for your device’s Management menu.
  4. Type U to Check for Software Updates.
  5. Your device should tell you that a new update is available and ask whether you would like to install it. Type Y to begin the installation.

Your device will download and install the update. Installation may take up to ten minutes.

When installation is complete, your device should restart automatically. If it does not, restart it using the power switch.

Better Feedback When Entering and Reading Numbers in Literary Braille

When entering numbers in literary Braille files, we now properly speak the letters following the number sign as numbers. This happens both when entering numbers and when reading them back one character at a time. In other words, typing a number sign followed by the letters abc will now properly speak those letters as 123.

Also, numbers with dashes or decimal points are now properly translated and spoken.

Direct Email Entry in U.S. Braille

Common lowercase email addresses can now be entered directly in U.S. literary Braille. Enter the at sign as Dot 4, then Dot 1. This direct email entry is a Blazie Technologies product convenience rather than part of official EBAE. Computer Braille remains recommended for entering email addresses; use a CBC span when the address must remain inside U.S. literary Braille and every character must be exact.

Extensive Improvements to English Braille

Braille accuracy when entering and reading text is substantially improved across the English tables. We have extensively updated the UEB Grade 2, U.S. Grade 2, U.S. Grade 1 and U.K. Grade 1 tables based on Liblouis 3.38.0.

  • Mixed letter-and-number strings, dates, times and identifiers such as R2D2 and SM7B can now be entered, spoken, copied and read back without letters or numbers being confused.
  • Literary Braille input and character-by-character speech now give more accurate feedback in the editor and dialog fields.
  • U.S., U.K. and UEB tables include numerous corrections, while U.S. Braille gains practical CBC entry and navigation for exact computer text.

Detailed English Braille improvements appear near the end of these release notes.

A More Responsive Set of DECtalk Voices

A newer version of the DECtalk voices is now available and more responsive. To use it, go to Options, Settings, Speech, Text to Speech Engine and choose DECtalk (via Speech Dispatcher).

With this speech engine, stopping the Say All command leaves the cursor on the last sentence spoken.

Problems that caused DECtalk speech to be cut off or pause unexpectedly have also been resolved.

Improvements to the Say All Command

Continuous reading with Dots 1-2-4-5-6-Chord now supports movement by line, paragraph, heading and block, as well as backward or forward by sentence. For example, press Dot 4-Chord to move to the next line while reading continues. Press Dots 7 and 8 together to stop reading.

Task Lists in the Editor

The Editor now supports Markdown task lists, providing a simple way to keep checklists in your documents.

Creating Task Lists Using the Navigation Menu
  • Create a file and write several lines of text, with one possible task on each line.
  • After entering the text, move the cursor onto the first line.
  • Open the Navigation menu with N-Chord (Dots 1-3-4-5) or CapsLock+N on a QWERTY keyboard.
  • Select Add or Toggle Task, or press T for the shortcut.
  • The Navigation menu closes, and the line becomes a task marked not done.
  • Move to the next line, reopen the Navigation menu and press T. Repeat these steps for each line you want to turn into a task.
  • To mark a task as being done, move to the line containing the task, reopen the Navigation menu and press T.
  • Repeating the command resets the task to not done.
  • To find unfinished tasks, reopen the Navigation menu and press P for the previous open task or Q for the next open task. Reopen the menu each time you want to move again.
  • To set a priority, move to a task, reopen the Navigation menu and press R.
  • Enter a letter such as A or B; earlier letters have higher priority, and Space clears the priority.

The Navigation menu also provides Mark All Tasks Done with A, Mark All Tasks Not Done with U, Set Task Due Date with D, Sort Tasks by Due Date with E, Sort Tasks by Priority with O, and Task Summary with S.

Sorting moves completed tasks to the bottom.

A blank line separates one task list from another. You can place a heading above the task list, and it will be associated with the list.

For complete instructions, press O-Chord, then H, choose Task Lists in the Editor, and press Enter. You can also press H-Chord while the Navigation menu is open for help with its task-list commands.

Manually Creating a Task with Markdown
  • Type a dash (Dots 3-6).
  • Type a space.
  • Type a left bracket (Dots 2-4-6-7).
  • Type either a space for a task that is not done or x for a completed task.
  • Type a right bracket (Dots 1-2-4-5-6-7).
  • Type a space, followed by the task text, such as “buy milk” or “complete my report”.

Examples:

– [ ] buy milk

– [x] send the letter

A space inside the brackets means that the task is not done, while x means the task is done.

When you use a task command, Markdown rendering turns on automatically so the Editor speaks the task’s state instead of reading the symbols.

Creating Links in a Document

Markdown links can now open a web page, another document or a specific location in the current document. A document link can target a heading, anchor or line number.

Creating a Link to a Web Page

To create a web link, press N-Chord to open the Navigation menu.

Choose Insert Web Link, or press W.

Enter the text you want the link to display.

Enter the web address. The field begins with https:// by default and the cursor is placed after it. Replace the prefix with http:// if the address requires it, then enter the rest of the address, such as www.blazietech.com. Press Enter or Tab when finished.

The address is validated. If it is valid, the device says “link inserted” and returns you to the document.

If it is invalid, you can return and correct it or choose to insert it anyway.

Note: Links use Markdown. Press Dot 8 with M to toggle Markdown rendering. When it is on, the device says “link” before the link label.

Creating Document Links

The Navigation menu can guide you through creating a document link.

Press N-Chord to open the Navigation menu.

Choose Insert Document Link, or press N.

Enter the link label, then press Enter or Tab.

Choose the file to link to.

The list contains currently open files. Select a file, or type the first few letters of its name to filter the list.

If required, you can also choose a heading in that file as the target.

The Navigation menu also has commands for the next link, previous link and return from an activated link. To return, press Dots 3-7-Chord.

Creating Email Links

Links can also use the mailto: prefix for creating a link to an email address. Activating an email link opens the Thunderbird email composer.

Email addresses are now validated before you can continue, and you can correct an invalid address.

Help and Documentation

Browse Help Topics by Category

Press O-Chord, then H, and choose Help Topics by Category. Press Enter to browse categories such as Getting Started, Keyboard and Input, Speech and Braille, etc.

New and Expanded On-Device Help
  • New on-device help explains editor links, task lists, and Using Braille on the BT Speak and BT Braille. The editor and Navigation menu help topics have also been updated and cross-linked to the relevant link, task-list and Braille Settings topics.
  • Customer-written apps can now supply their own help directory, so pressing H-Chord inside them opens their own help rather than the general help.
  • The Menu Navigation help topic now contains additional details.
Documentation and Language Improvements
  • German, French and Spanish help topics have also been reformatted for more consistent and accessible reading.
  • Spacing and layout corrections throughout the help topics, the German and French user manuals, and the BT Code lessons make them read more cleanly.

Other Fixes and Improvements

AI Tools and Performance
Faster Loading of Apps
  • Apps in Blazie mode now start noticeably faster, including Bard, BT Code, Calendar, Dictionary, Morse, Podcasts, Radio Tuner, Smart Help and Voice Notes, saving roughly 300 milliseconds on launch.
A Faster Way to Access AI Tools

You can now Press E-Chord with Dot 8 to open the AI Tools menu directly, rather than having to first open the main Editor menu.

Improvements to AI Responses
  • AI responses now contain Markdown-formatted links that can be opened from the AI result viewer. Place the cursor on a link and press J with dot 8, or Alt+J on a QWERTY keyboard, to follow it.
  • You can now press dots 7 and 8 together to stop speech in an AI response.
Editor and File Browser
Improvements to the File Browser
  • Files that are open in the editor can no longer be changed from the File Browser. This includes deleting, renaming, protecting or unprotecting the file. For example, if you try to delete a file which is opened in the editor, a warning reminds you that the file is still open. Once you close the file, you will then be able to make these changes.

To close a file from the Editor, press E-Chord, choose Close Current File, or press C. This saves any changes and closes the file.

Close All Open Files

In the Editor menu, Close All Files, shortcut L, immediately closes all open files and returns you to the Welcome screen.

Apps, Media and Storage
Fixes to NFB Newsline
  • Newsline catalog loading and publication searches are faster and handle malformed service data more reliably. Problems affecting automatic Newsline downloads have also been fixed.
  • Downloaded publications are reformatted for easier reading.
  • Markdown headings now identify the publication, its sections and individual articles, making it easier to move through a publication with heading navigation commands.
Improvements to the Radio Tuner
  • In the radio tuner, recordings made from the ACB Media menu, and from other stations, were saved as .ts files which could not be played. This is now fixed. Recordings are saved in their proper format, so a station that broadcasts in MP3, such as any of the ACB Media channels, is now recorded as a genuine MP3 file. As a bonus, the size of the recording is about a third smaller than before. Recordings you made before installing this update are not changed, so those will still need to be renamed with an .mp4 extension if you want to keep them.
  • Stations opened from the built-in station menus, such as the Blindness Community stations, are now recognized as stations from the other menus, allowing you to vote for those stations, as well.
Media, USB Storage and Speech Synthesizers
  • Pausing or resuming media with Dots 1-2-5-6-Chord (the ou sign) now responds in about 15 milliseconds instead of 250 milliseconds.
  • Media files and folders containing square brackets, asterisks or question marks in their names can now be played correctly.
  • We fixed the problem where USB drives and SD cards were appearing in the file browser, even after those drives were ejected or removed. Once a drive is removed or ejected, those entries are now automatically removed.
  • Problems uninstalling speech synthesizers have been fixed. If the selected synthesizer is currently in use, the device now explains that you must choose another synthesizer first. Saved profiles that would prevent successful removal are handled automatically.
Speech, Braille and Navigation
  • Dynamic menus, such as Speech Controls, now interrupt earlier speech and announce the new menu as soon as it opens.
  • Words typed in all capitals are now read the same way in dialog boxes as they are in the editor.
  • Spelling a word now tells you about capitals. Press dots 2-5 chord repeatedly to read the word, spell it, then spell it in the spelling alphabet. The spelling alphabet now says “cap” before a capital letter and announces “all caps” once for a word written entirely in capitals.
  • A cell that is part of a contraction is no longer named as the first letter of the word the contraction stands for. Moving over the cell that spells “blind” used to say “b”; it is now read as the Braille character it actually is.
  • Entering data into LibreOffice Calc with Braille input (Dots 3-5-8-Chord) no longer sends the cursor back to cell A1.
Device, Localization and Reliability
Agenda Calendar and Time Zone Fixes
  • Agenda event times are now communicated correctly.
  • Changing the time zone now keeps the device’s time zone records synchronized. This prevents conflicting time zone information from causing date-parsing problems.
Device Updates
  • The updater is much faster now and provides clearer announcements about the current stage of the update process.
General Improvements
  • Dates written in ISO form (year-month-day) are now always accepted, whichever country your device is set to.
  • Non-English confirmation questions now use the correct keys. In German, for example, the device asks for J or N rather than Y or N, so Shut Down, Restart and other confirmation questions work correctly.
  • More of the interface has been localized: some strings that could never be translated before are now translated, and corruption in several existing translations was fixed in German, French and Portuguese.
  • The vibrations now stop reliably when an app exits, and vibrate can be given a value of 0 to stop it immediately.
  • A clearer message is now given when the time zone lookup service is busy and refuses the request, instead of a generic failure.
  • Installation and storage preparation now work correctly when the device uses a non-English locale.
  • The Italian Braille table was renamed in Liblouis 3.38 and the setting has been updated to match, so Italian Braille keeps working after the upgrade.
  • The battery voltage reference has been recalibrated against the MAX17260 fuel gauge for more accurate readings.
BT Braille Improvements
  • Plugging headphones into the 3.5 mm jack now mutes the built-in speaker.
  • When accessing certain BRF files, Dot 7 is now removed from certain Braille characters.
  • Audio recovery is more reliable when the internal bus misbehaves or audio is lost on certain kernel versions.
  • The BT Braille battery gauge now resets its state of charge correctly after reinitialization or recalibration.
  • Panning left no longer skips the capital letter at the start of a line.
  • Panning at the end of a file now stops instead of wrapping to the beginning of the line.
  • A rare problem that prevented some key sequences from being recognized has been fixed, particularly for O-Chord, L1-R3 and the cursor routing keys.
  • The correct internal sound device is now selected for each product, and reset-audio-sink has been corrected.
  • Pico firmware has been updated to version 0.48, improving correlation between Pico and CM5 battery reporting.
  • BT Braille now reliably announces that it is ready after a full startup.
Detailed English Braille Improvements
General Braille Accuracy and Input Improvements
  • Mixed letter-and-number strings, dates, times, decimals, addresses, slash-separated and hyphenated groups, and identifiers are now more likely to remain correct when entered, spoken, copied or read back.
  • Dotted abbreviations and initialisms such as e.g., i.e., U.S., Ph.D., SD and LLC are preserved more accurately. Link targets such as file:/, view:/ and audio:/ are preserved, and compact dot-number labels such as Dot 3456 are no longer read as “ble” in the legacy U.K. and U.S. Grade 1 tables.
  • Literary Braille single characters are now decoded and spoken correctly for the full character set, not just numbers and capital letters, both as you type them and when reading them back, in the editor and in dialog boxes.
U.S. Braille Improvements
  • In U.S. Braille, instructions ending with a named letter now retain the required letter sign. For example, “press the letter r.” no longer comes back as “press the letter rather”.
U.K. Braille Improvements
  • In U.K. Braille, attached commas, semicolons, colons, full stops, exclamation marks and question marks now return as punctuation instead of being reported as numbers or unrelated contractions. If you had poor results with the U.K. table in the past, please try it again; numerous Braille accuracy problems have been corrected.
Email Addresses and Exact Text
  • Email addresses, web addresses and supported links are preserved more reliably in both U.S. Braille and UEB, including their punctuation, common suffixes and link targets.
  • Some URLs, web addresses, email addresses, paths and similar exact content may be stored inside Computer Braille Code spans in a U.S. literary Braille document. CBC uses its own start and end indicators and is not the same as eight-dot Computer Braille. See the detailed CBC section near the end of these release notes.
Using Computer Braille Code (CBC) in U.S. Braille

Computer Braille Code, or CBC, is a six-dot code for exact computer text within U.S. literary Braille. It is different from the device’s eight-dot Computer Braille mode, is not selected as a Braille table, and is currently supported within one logical line.

URLs, email addresses, paths, filenames, commands and code may appear inside a CBC span.

CBC Quick Reference
  • Start CBC with Dots 4-5-6, then Dots 3-4-6.
  • End CBC with Dots 4-5-6, then Dots 1-5-6.
  • Move through the stored cells with Dot 3-Chord or Dot 6-Chord, and speak the current cell with Dots 3-6-Chord.
  • Data cells are spoken as their computer characters. Capital, emphasis, continuation and span indicators are spoken as dot shapes.
Entering CBC Data
  • Inside a CBC span, enter lowercase letters, digits and punctuation with familiar six-dot Computer Braille cells. Most are the same as eight-dot Computer Braille, but some symbols differ.
  • Add Dot 7 to a letter for a capital. The device stores the official two-cell CBC capital form and treats it as one input action for undo.
  • CBC entry supports common computer symbols including the at sign, brackets, backslash, braces, caret, vertical bar, grave accent, tilde and underscore. The on-device Braille help gives the exact cells and shifted pairs.
  • Enter every required space because spacing is significant in computer text.
Capital Letters
  • For multiple capitals, start capital lock with Dots 4-5-6, then Dots 3-4-5.
  • Enter the letters using their lowercase cells.
  • Release capital lock with Dots 4-5-6, then Dots 1-2-6.

Capital lock also ends at the next significant space or the CBC end indicator.

For complete guidance, including exact symbol forms, see the Using Braille help topic for your device in the on-device help.

Contact Information

Blazie Technologies

Email: info@blazie.net

Phone: (772) 214-1616

Web: www.blazietech.com

It doesn’t include the features you rely on every day. Or it has keys you hardly ever use. So you adapt. But honestly, you shouldn’t have to. Because everyone works differently, learns differently … Continue reading From Help Tech GmbH: myBraille is live: Configure your Braille display your way
item.content:encoded:
Your braille display shouldn’t decide. You should.

Maybe you’ve experienced it. Your braille display is a little too large to carry around.

It doesn’t include the features you rely on every day. Or it has keys you hardly ever use.

So you adapt. But honestly, you shouldn’t have to. Because everyone works differently, learns differently and reads differently.

So why should the same braille display be the right choice for everyone?

Find out more on the Help Tech Blog

item.title: From HumanWare: 2027 Product pricing update
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: At HumanWare, our mission is to develop innovative assistive technology that empowers people who are blind or have low vision to live more independently. We are equally committed to being open and transparent with our customers and partners, which is why we want to provide advance notice of an upcoming pricing adjustment affecting select products. … Continue reading From HumanWare: 2027 Product pricing update
item.content:encoded:
At HumanWare, our mission is to develop innovative assistive technology that empowers people who are blind or have low vision to live more independently. We are equally committed to being open and transparent with our customers and partners, which is why we want to provide advance notice of an upcoming pricing adjustment affecting select products.

Over the past year, the cost of key electronic components used in our products, including memory and storage, has increased significantly across the technology industry. While we have worked hard to absorb these rising costs wherever possible, continued increases require us to adjust pricing on selected products.

This decision was not made lightly as we strive to offer solutions at the best possible price. The adjustment will help ensure we can continue delivering the innovation, product quality, reliability, software improvements, and customer support that our customers and partners have come to expect from HumanWare.

The updated pricing will take effect on January 1, 2027. Orders placed on or before December 31, 2026, will continue to receive current pricing.

We sincerely appreciate your continued trust and partnership. Thank you for your ongoing support of HumanWare. If you have any questions about these changes, please contact your HumanWare representative.

This limited-time trade-in program is expected to … Continue reading From HumanWare: Trade in and Save on BrailleNote Evolve
item.content:encoded:
Now is the perfect time to move to the next generation of braille notetaking and computing. For a limited time, trade in your BrailleNote Touch Plus 32 or BrailleSense 6 and receive:

  • £1,000 toward a new BrailleNote evolve 32
  • £500 toward a new BrailleNote evolve 20

This trade-in program helps you upgrade to BrailleNote evolve while saving on your purchase.

Don’t wait. This limited-time trade-in program is expected to end at the end of 2026. We encourage you to take advantage of this opportunity while trade-in credits remain available.

This program is about more than upgrading technology.

Every eligible BrailleNote Touch Plus collected through this initiative will be donated through HumanWare’s Emerging Braille Program, helping students and individuals in developing countries gain access to braille technology that might otherwise be out of reach.

A braille device can open doors to education, employment, and independence. Stories like Erik’s remind us how a single tool can help build a brighter future.

Trade-ins are not available for online orders. To take advantage of this offer, please contact your local HumanWare team.

item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The BT Braille is a powerful, Braille first computer with an eight-dot Braille keyboard with speech and Braille output in 20 cell and 40 cell models. This device can be as simple as being your trusty notetaker but it’s powerful enough for those who want to write their own code and run your own software. … Continue reading Tek Talk welcomes David Goldfield, Blindness Assistive Technology Specialist, to discuss the BT Braille, Tuesday 11 August at 1:00 AM
item.content:encoded:
The BT Braille is a powerful, Braille first computer with an eight-dot Braille keyboard with speech and Braille output in 20 cell and 40 cell models. This device can be as simple as being your trusty notetaker but it’s powerful enough for those who want to write their own code and run your own software. It has more features than you can shake a white cane at. To name a few, it has a phone book, appointment calendar, calculator, stopwatch, an email program, two Web browsers, a radio tuner, a YouTube app and more. We can’t wait to tell you more about the BT Braille and answer your questions about it.

item.content:encoded:
Trans-Tasman Certificate of Proficiency in Unified English Braille Jointly administered by The Braille Authority of New Zealand Aotearoa Trust and Australian Braille Authority

2026 Invitation

Closing Date: Monday 31 August 2026

Attention Braille Teachers, Transcribers and Users

You are warmly invited to apply to sit the Trans-Tasman Certificate of Proficiency in Unified English Braille. All the details about the Certificate are on the BANZAT website at https://www.banzat.org.nz/trans-tasman-certificate-of-proficiency-in-unified-english-braille

The link to the application form is at the foot of the page on the website.

The Certificate in UEB is an open book examination which should be completed without conferring with others. The timetable for the examination is on the website.

Practice papers and the New Zealand edition of the UEB Manual are also available on the BANZAT website at https://www.banzat.org.nz/trans-tasman-certificate-of-proficiency-in-unified-english-braille

For further information or any queries please contact the examinations Committee, email exam@banzat.org.nz or phone 0800 BANZAT (0800 226928)

We warmly welcome your applications. Applications close on Monday 31 August 2026.

If you’re attending, be sure to visit Selvas BLV at Booth 400 to experience the all-new BrailleSense 7. BrailleSense 7 preorder

item.content:encoded:
Join David Goldfield for our next Blazie Technologies Training Session!

In this session, you’ll learn how to confidently browse the web using BT Speak and BT Braille. David will cover the differences between Chromium and Firefox, navigating webpages with browse mode and quick navigation keys, working with forms, understanding focus mode, using the address bar, and configuring Orca for the best browsing experience.

We certainly won’t be able to cover everything in one session, but our hope is that when the session has ended that you’ll have the confidence to start browsing the Web on your Blazie device.

item.title: Braille on the Mac, Tuesday at 7:30 PM
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Over the years, we have extensively covered various aspects of using braille displays with iPhones and iPads. However, Apple doesn’t just make smartphones and tablets! VoiceOver first came to the Apple Macintosh line of desktop and laptop computers in 2005, and it now boasts support for a wide array of braille displays, including many which … Continue reading Braille on the Mac, Tuesday at 7:30 PM
item.content:encoded:
Over the years, we have extensively covered various aspects of using braille displays with iPhones and iPads. However, Apple doesn’t just make smartphones and tablets!

VoiceOver first came to the Apple Macintosh line of desktop and laptop computers in 2005, and it now boasts support for a wide array of braille displays, including many which are no longer supported on Windows.

In this session, we are delighted to be joined by Marco Zehe, an accessibility specialist who uses braille on the Mac on a day-to-day basis. Marco will explain and demonstrate:

  • How to connect braille displays to the Mac
  • Common braille display commands
  • Braille settings
  • How braille on the Mac compares with braille on iOS

We look forward to your company at this long overdue session!

Register for Braille on the Mac

item.title: From Jonathan Mosen: With Gratitude and Appreciation, Remembering Access Technology Great Jonathan Sharp
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: I think most of us like to hope that when our time is up, in some small way, we will have left this world having made it a better place. Jonathan Sharp, who died last Sunday at the age of 67 after a lengthy illness, was an exceptionally quiet, humble man. Yet he vastly improved … Continue reading From Jonathan Mosen: With Gratitude and Appreciation, Remembering Access Technology Great Jonathan Sharp
item.content:encoded:
I think most of us like to hope that when our time is up, in some small way, we will have left this world having made it a better place. Jonathan Sharp, who died last Sunday at the age of 67 after a lengthy illness, was an exceptionally quiet, humble man. Yet he vastly improved the lives of blind people worldwide, even though most of them may not know his name.

This brilliant new Zealander was unquestionably one of the giants of the blindness technology pioneers, and arguably the most unassuming of all of them. Those of us who know our blindness technology history refer to Jonathan as “the father of KeySoft”, the software package that has powered many products released by Wormald International Sensory Aids, Pulse Data International, and now HumanWare. There is no other person who could possibly claim that title.

Jonathan was hired in the 1980s by the brilliant access technology entrepreneur Russell Smith. His first project was to take an off-the-shelf Epson HX-20, and develop something revolutionary – a portable talking computer that a blind person could use. When I say portable, by the time Wormald International Sensory Aids had done all the necessary modifications, it weighed about six pounds. But the independence it facilitated was so profound that I don’t remember anyone complaining about the weight. If a blind person was fortunate enough to own one of these devices, gone were the days when a blind person had to Braille their work, then type it for a sighted teacher or colleague, without being able to verify what they had typed, or even if the ribbon had run out. Instead, blind people would be able to write, format, edit and then print or emboss their own documents.

It is important to put this development into historical context, because it makes it all the more remarkable. Jonathan developed this tool in an era when most households didn’t own a computer, and laptops for business users were practically unheard of. Thanks to him, blind people were using an effective portable solution well ahead of such products being available generally.

Clearly there were technical issues to resolve, and I don’t downplay the significance of those. But where Jonathan was exceptional, where his genius really showed, was in his ability to create elegant user experiences. Jonathan, who was not blind, did it by doing a lot of listening, and then asking more thoughtful, probing questions. He never assumed that he knew what was best for blind people. Perhaps nudged along regularly by one of Russell’s favorite questions, “how hard can it be”, he turned blind people’s dreams into a tangible product we could use.

In 1986, every character of code was precious, because space was so limited. Yet Jonathan set out to create a device that anyone could use. You didn’t have to be technically inclined to use a Keynote.

There were three secret ingredients to Jonathan’s recipe.

First, an intuitive menu-driven system. Arrow through your selections, or use first letter navigation, plus plenty of shortcuts for those who prioritized efficiency.

Second, consistency. Long before graphical user interfaces were commonplace, Jonathan had worked out that if you want a user interface to be intuitive, you had to make sure that whenever possible, things worked the same way across applications.

Third, and most important, remarkably comprehensive context-sensitive help. The detail in that help was truly extraordinary. It meant that someone who might in the past have been frightened of computers could learn at their own place and pace, and would soon be writing beautifully-formatted documents.

I suppose that after having rescued a few teachers from the vagaries of our Apple IIE installation which included a VersaBraille, it was decided that I might be a good test case to use a Keynote for my schooling to see what happened. This I duly did starting in 1986. It may not surprise many people to know that I had a few opinions about how the software might be improved, and it was these opinions that were held with the forthrightness and certainty common to many teenagers that connected me with Jonathan Sharp.

I was in awe of Jonathan. He would have been in his mid-20s when I got to know him, and to my teenage self, he was like this magician who made incredible things happen. I cringe a little now when I think of the time I would spend making a long distance call to him, me in Auckland, he in Christchurch, and how much of his time I would occupy. He was incredibly patient and polite, treating me with courtesy even though I’m sure some of my ideas were completely uninformed and ridiculous.

I do have a favorite Jonathan story from this era. One day at school, I made a discovery that very much appealed to my teenage self, and couldn’t wait to get home so I could call Jonathan to show it to him. The original Keynote contained a row of function keys, one of which was the keyboard voice button. If you pressed it, the voice, which was based on the Artic Technologies 263 chip back then, would say, “keyboard voice, currently…” and then whatever the voice was set to. At this point, you had three choices. If you pressed the letter f, you would turn the keyboard echo completely off. If you pressed W, you would set it to word echo. And if you pressed S, you would set it to spell, which echoed every character. So I called Jonathan, with my Keynote keyboard voice set to spell, and I breathlessly said, “hey Jonathan! Listen to this! This is so cool!” And I pressed the keyboard voice button which confirmed that it was set to spell, so it was echoing every character. Then I pressed the key to turn keyboard echo off, F. And the keynote said, “F, off”. Well, Jonathan must have been utterly mortified, because when I got home from school the next day, a floppy disk was waiting for me in the mail, and after I installed the software update it contained, it wouldn’t say “F, off” anymore. Jonathan had obviously put the phone down and taken care of it right away.

Even in the early days of Keynote, it was possible to install third-party utilities, although there was no publicly available software development kit. Jonathan wrote a little app for the Keynote called KeyTerm which changed my life. He explained to me what a modem was, and what I could do if I bought one. I had to try. So, I bought a modem, fired up KeyTerm, and never looked back. I used it to connect at considerable expense to the CompuServe information Service, and that is how I discovered the National Federation of the Blind, which transformed my life even from half a world away.

Eventually, the rest of the world caught up with what blind people were already doing, and laptops became more common. Jonathan ported KeySoft to DOS, allowing it to run on a Toshiba laptop, and exit to DOS where you could run any application you liked.

Many people are not aware of Jonathan’s remarkable contribution to the screen reader industry. Pulse Data International developed a screen reader for DOS computers called MasterTouch. It worked particularly well with the Keynote Gold speech synthesizer, which, while perhaps an acquired taste like a lot of text-to-speech of that era, had accurate pronunciation, was highly responsive, and intelligible at fast speeds. If you remember the DOS screen reader era, you may recall that there were two common methods of writing text to the screen. If text was written through the computer’s BIOS, screen readers had no difficulty speaking text automatically. However, increasingly, developers wrote software using direct screen writes. While faster, text written this way could not be spoken automatically by most DOS screen readers and required some sort of review technique. Jonathan was able to find a way around that. MasterTouch was one of only a small number of screen readers that automatically spoke direct screen written text.

Another innovative element of MasterTouch was its optional touch tablet, long before the era of touch screens we take for granted today. Because screens in those days were a predictable 25 lines by 80 characters, Pulse Data developed a device that let you run your fingers across the virtual screen, and hear the characters under your fingers. It played a critical role in giving those of us who were users spatial awareness of the way the screen was laid out.

All this in the early 1990s. If you used a software application often enough, you could get very efficient working this way, because you could place your finger where you knew relevant text would appear. It was well ahead of its time. Touch the screen to find out what was there. Typical of Jonathan’s work, it contained robust context-sensitive help, so people could learn the system.

Jonathan continued to quietly change the world. He played a pivotal role in creating the underlying architecture and expanding software feature set of BrailleNote, the first version of which was released in 2000, powered by Windows CE. With that strong KeySoft inheritance at its core, it was utterly disruptive, becoming the dominant player in that market segment in a remarkably short time.

Jonathan was instrumental in changing the way blind people travel, working with Mike May and Charles LaPierre of the Sendero Group to bring truly portable GPS-based navigation to the blind. With care and thought, he brought an external package into the BrailleNote family in a way that preserved the user interface elements that were so critical to the BrailleNote’s success. We take it for granted now, but it is hard to overstate the sense of awe many of us felt at being able to ride a bus or taxi, or walk an unfamiliar street, and be told all the businesses we were passing and the names of the streets we were approaching.

When Pulse Data started sounding me out in 2003 about managing their blindness products, working with Jonathan, someone I viewed as a hero and a mentor, was a massive drawcard. In the three years that I worked closely with Jonathan, he taught me so much. I was the product manager, and I had opinions. Sometimes, Jonathan would enthusiastically work with me to realize what customers were telling me was needed. At other times, he would challenge me to think differently about the need for a feature, or the way I wanted it to work. When he did so, he almost always had the better idea, and when Jonathan spoke, I knew it was right to always listen. But he also knew that as one of KeySoft’s original users, I got the paradigm he had created. We made remarkable progress during that time. We worked with Baum’s hardware to produce the cute and powerful BrailleNote PK, added a raft of new features to KeySoft, and of course the crowning glory, BrailleNote mPower, which no one knew about until the day it was ready to ship.

Jonathan continued to make a difference for many years, and his clarity of thought around user interface for blind people has impacted products well beyond those he developed directly.

I kept in touch with Jonathan from time to time and we would reminisce about the old days. He would kindly reach out every so often, just to check in.

The Blind community has lost one of the greatest technologists that has ever worked with us. The world has lost a gentle, humble, good soul. But I know that Jonathan would want me to mention those he loved. Let us extend our love and condolences to Heloise, Julia and Peter, Nick and Grace, Joseph, Susanna, Lois, and David.

Last year, I was contacted by a teacher in New Zealand named Ruth, who asked if I would speak virtually to her class. It turns out she is Jonathan’s niece. It wasn’t until she read my tribute on the 20th anniversary of Russell Smith’s death that she gained a greater understanding of what a significant figure in blindness technology Jonathan is. I can well imagine that. He never tooted his own horn.

It will not be a comfort now as the family grieves, but I hope in time, they will take great pride in the fact that Jonathan changed the world for the better. Many blind people pursued an education more successfully, or held down a job, or realized with delight that they could use a computer after all, specifically because of Jonathan Sharp. I am sorry beyond words that he has gone, but that is one amazing legacy to leave.

Thank you for everything, Jonathan. I will miss you very much, but it was an honor to know you.

item.title: Blazie Technologies Announces Legacy Trade-In Program for Blazie Engineering Products
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Blazie Technologies is pleased to announce its new Legacy Trade-In Program, giving customers the opportunity to receive $200 off the purchase of a new Blazie Technologies product when they trade in an eligible Blazie Engineering product. For years, Blazie Engineering products have earned a reputation for accessibility, reliability, and durability. Many of those devices remain … Continue reading Blazie Technologies Announces Legacy Trade-In Program for Blazie Engineering Products
item.content:encoded:
Blazie Technologies is pleased to announce its new Legacy Trade-In Program, giving customers the opportunity to receive $200 off the purchase of a new Blazie Technologies product when they trade in an eligible Blazie Engineering product.

For years, Blazie Engineering products have earned a reputation for accessibility, reliability, and durability. Many of those devices remain in use today, reflecting the lasting quality of the products. We know these products are important to our customers, and they are important to us as well. The Legacy Trade-In Program recognizes that shared history by honoring the lasting value of Blazie Engineering products and the customers who have relied on them for years.

“Our customers have always been at the heart of everything we do,” said Bryan Blazie, Chief Executive Officer of Blazie Technologies. “Many people are still using products originally purchased from Blazie Engineering, and we want them to know that those products still hold value. This program is our way of thanking our longtime customers and recognizing the investment they’ve made in our products.”

Through the Legacy Trade-In Program, customers will receive $200 off the purchase of one Blazie Technologies product when they trade in one eligible Blazie Engineering product. Trade-in products do not need to be operational to qualify. Only one qualifying trade-in may be applied per eligible product purchase, and there is no expiration date for the program.

Eligible trade-in products include: Braille ‘n Speak Classic, Braille ‘n Speak 640, and Braille ‘n Speak 2000; Type ‘n Speak; Type Lite; all Braille Lite models, including Braille Lite 18 and Braille Lite 40; and Braille Blazer embosser. Accessories, including carrying cases, cables, cassette tape interfaces, disk drive accessories, and standalone disk drives, are not eligible for the program. The Braille ‘n Speak Scholar from APH is also not eligible for the Legacy Trade-In Program.

The products may have changed, but our commitment to our customers has not. From our Blazie family to yours, we look forward to reconnecting with you.

For additional information about the Legacy Trade-In Program or to confirm product eligibility, contact Blazie Technologies at (772) 214-1616 or fill out our Legacy form.

item.title: From Selvas: Important Announcement About USB Braille Driver for Windows
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We would like to share with you an important issue regarding our USB Braille display driver with Windows. As of the most recent Windows update, our legacy USB drivers have been disabled due to outdated security certificates. We are currently addressing this problem with Microsoft and hope to have a fix soon. This affects our … Continue reading From Selvas: Important Announcement About USB Braille Driver for Windows
item.content:encoded: We would like to share with you an important issue regarding our USB Braille display driver with Windows. As of the most recent Windows update, our legacy USB drivers have been disabled due to outdated security certificates. We are currently addressing this problem with Microsoft and hope to have a fix soon. This affects our BrailleSense 6 line, the QBraille, and other older Braille displays over USB. These devices can still be used over Bluetooth, and the eMotion and the new BrailleSense 7 are not affected at all, as they do not use these drivers. We recognize the serious and widespread nature of this problem, and we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience this is causing our users. We will update you with a fix as soon as possible.

item.title: From Selvas: Release of New Apps for BrailleSense
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: SELVAS is thrilled to announce the availability of 3 new apps for the BrailleSense 6 and 6 mini, all of which can be downloaded via the optional Add-Ons menu. 1.      New web TV App 2.      New Play store search add-on 3.      Words With HIMS Add-On The Web browser V2 add-on has also been updated to … Continue reading From Selvas: Release of New Apps for BrailleSense
item.content:encoded:
SELVAS is thrilled to announce the availability of 3 new apps for the BrailleSense 6 and 6 mini, all of which can be downloaded via the optional Add-Ons menu.

1.      New web TV App

  1. Installs to the Media menu below web Radio.
  2. Contains the same exact interface as the Web Radio, but for freely available online TV stations.
  3. Uses an Open Source database that is actively maintained. Thus, be sure to update the database often, and to know that, if stations stop working, they may well return in a few days.

2.      New Play store search add-on

  1. Installs to the Android Apps menu below the Play Store.
  2. This program creates a BrailleSense-type interface for searching applications on the Play Store. However, as with Video search and YouTube, the Play store page is opened for installation.
  3. When you open the program, you are offered options for searching by keyword or category. Keyword asks you to type a search term, while category offers a list of categories. As with other search programs, Tab to reach more specific information, and Shift-Tab to return to more general designations.
  4. When in a list of results, press Enter-I to get information about the application.
  5. Press Enter on the focused application to open its page in the Play store to install it. Remember that you can use first letter navigation here, and pressing the letter I a time or two should get you to the Install button. Aside from direct installation, you shouldn’t need to interact directly with the Play store interface.

3.      Words With HIMS Add-On

  1. This is a general word game of words of different lengths and clues. Installs to the Extras Menu.
  2. Be sure to use Tab and Shift-Tab to discover all the current controls and information.
  3. In addition to the included words and clues, you can also add your own, and set several options for play.

The Web browser V2 add-on has also been updated to fix several reported issues. Other add-ons have been updated to reflect refinements in Braille translation, but do not contain additional features and functions.

item.title: From Orbit Research: Firmware Version B0.xx.00.69rxx is now available for the Orbit Reader 20
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We are pleased to announce the release of firmware version B0.xx.00.69rxx for the Orbit Reader 20. Following are the new features and improvements. Notes: Please note that if the device’s current firmware version is B0.xx.00.69r36 or an earlier version, following points must be considered: The firmware package can be downloaded from our website’s Support menu. … Continue reading From Orbit Research: Firmware Version B0.xx.00.69rxx is now available for the Orbit Reader 20
item.content:encoded:
We are pleased to announce the release of firmware version B0.xx.00.69rxx for the Orbit Reader 20.

Following are the new features and improvements.

  1. Added support for setting the Orbit Reader 20 device nickname using the Orbit Chat app.
  2. Resolved an issue affecting the naming of files received from the Orbit Chat app.

Notes:

Please note that if the device’s current firmware version is B0.xx.00.69r36 or an earlier version, following points must be considered:

  1. The device settings will be reset to their defaults after the upgrade.
  2. If localization has been applied, you will also need to re-apply it after the upgrade using the package available on our website at https://www.orbitresearch.com/support/orbit-reader-20-support/#LocalizationPackage

The firmware package can be downloaded from our website’s Support menu.

To identify the proper firmware package for your unit, you will need to check the version number of the firmware currently loaded on your unit. If your unit does not turn on or if you are not able to read the version number from your device, please contact our technical support team at techsupport@orbitresearch.com.

To check the version number of your current firmware package please follow the following steps:

  1. Power ON your unit.
  2. Press the Select + Up key to open the menu.
  3. Scroll down to the item “Ver.” by pressing down the arrow key.
  4. It should display the firmware version number on your Braille display.

Check the first four digits of the version number and click on the respective link in the table on our website to download the appropriate firmware package. Once downloaded, you can install it using the SD card method or using the Windows utility program.

The firmware package is available here – https://www.orbitresearch.com/support/orbit-reader-20-support/orbit-reader-firmware-download/

The Localization package is available here – https://www.orbitresearch.com/support/orbit-reader-20-support/#LocalizationPackage For instructions on upgrading the Orbit Reader 21, please refer to Section 21 of the User Guide available on the website at https://www.orbitresearch.com/support/orbit-reader-20-support/orbit-reader-20-user-guide-downloads/

item.title: From Harri Pasanen: MBraille Windows Desktop version refresh available
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: I updated MBraille Desktop for Windows.  This release is now fully self-voicing, as NVDA and JAWS had trouble navigating it fully.  So the advice is to suspend those while using MBraille. Windows version is a free application. If you don’t know what MBraille is, below is a “pitch” MBraille is an innovative typing and notetaking … Continue reading From Harri Pasanen: MBraille Windows Desktop version refresh available
item.content:encoded:
I updated MBraille Desktop for Windows.  This release is now fully self-voicing, as NVDA and JAWS had trouble navigating it fully.  So the advice is to suspend those while using MBraille.

Windows version is a free application.

If you don’t know what MBraille is, below is a “pitch”

MBraille is an innovative typing and notetaking application designed to let you type in braille using standard hardware. It bridges the gap between traditional braille writing and everyday modern technology, allowing blind, visually impaired, or sighted individuals learning braille to type efficiently without needing expensive, specialized braille hardware.

What It Does & How It Works

Standard Key Mapping: The application turns a regular QWERTY keyboard (or a mobile touchscreen) into a braille input device. It maps the standard 6-dot braille cell to six home-row keys: S, D, F represent dots 1, 2, and 3 (left hand), and J, K, L represent dots 4, 5, and 6 (right hand). You press these keys simultaneously to input characters.

Speech Feedback & Screen Reader Integration: As you type, MBraille provides immediate audio feedback, reading back letters, words, and commands. On desktop platforms like Windows, it integrates seamlessly with leading screen readers such as NVDA and JAWS.

Support for Multiple Formats: It supports both contracted (shorthand/Grade 2) and uncontracted (character-by-character/Grade 1) braille across many different languages.

Core Features

Learning & Skill Building: The desktop version includes guided exercises specifically designed to help beginners master the 6-dot system, build muscle memory, and improve typing fluency.

Rich Text Editing & Utilities: Beyond simple entry, it offers full word-processing capabilities including cursor movement, text selection, copy/cut/paste, undo, search, and bookmarking.

A Mobile Powerhouse: While the Windows version acts as an excellent training ground and stationary desk tool, MBraille transforms on iOS and Android. On mobile devices, it operates as a full-fledged, braille-first notetaker. It allows you to use the touchscreen for chorded braille entry, utilize voice dictation, use a one-handed mode, and use specific braille command shortcuts to send texts, make phone calls, and manage daily tasks.

Cloud Connectivity: The platform syncs seamlessly with popular cloud storage services like Dropbox, Google Drive, and OneDrive so you can access your notes across devices.

Who Is It For?

MBraille is ideal for individuals who are blind or visually impaired looking for a fast, “eyes-free” way to type on everyday devices without carrying heavy external braille displays. It is also an excellent tool for educators, students, or anyone wanting to learn the mechanics of braille typing.

MBraille is localized to 24 languages.

item.title: From APH: Announcing BrailleBlaster 3.2.2
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: Welcome to BrailleBlaster 3.2.2. This release has improvements with tables and with the backspace and delete keys. This release is now available to download from the BrailleBlaster website. Bug Fixes and Improvements
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to BrailleBlaster 3.2.2. This release has improvements with tables and with the backspace and delete keys. This release is now available to download from the BrailleBlaster website.

Bug Fixes and Improvements

  • The Ctrl+End and Ctrl+Home Keystrokes and Hot Keys are functioning normally.
  • Able to open file with a definition list that is using Pandoc Importer.
  • In tables the last column is blank, and guide dots are now being shown in the last column to show as empty.
  • Two-rowed table cells have correct widths in the table.
  • Alt text is working accordingly. There are transcriber notes visible in the braille view for when there is alt text seen.
  • Customer service issue where the backspace button was not functioning properly has been fixed.
  • Customer service issue where deleting five lines at the top of a document cause an exception error has been fixed.
  • Copying for internal documents matches style from one document to another.
  • The page break drifting up as typing is no longer occurring. The difficulty typing before the page break has been fixed.
  • List paragraph style from Word will convert to list braille content as it should.
  • No longer seeing the Displayed Blocked Text in Style View.
  • Opening a bad filename at the C Prompt is now fixed.
  • Imported Math has all characters and exhibits a completed equation from a ASCIIMath rendering.
  • Brailleblaster Quick Reference Card.brf file is embossable on Pageblasters embossers.
  • MathML is working accordingly.
  • A number of other minor improvements and bug fixes.

item.title: TAVIP Masterclass: The Canute Scientific from Bristol Braille, Tuesday 14 July at 7:30 PM
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: We are pleased to promote this event from TAVIP as an alternative to our Braille Bar which is taking place at the same time. From TAVIP: I am pleased to invite you to a TAVIP Masterclass with Ed Rogers from Bristol Braille who will be talking about the development and launch of the Canute Scientific. … Continue reading TAVIP Masterclass: The Canute Scientific from Bristol Braille, Tuesday 14 July at 7:30 PM
item.content:encoded:
We are pleased to promote this event from TAVIP as an alternative to our Braille Bar which is taking place at the same time. From TAVIP:

I am pleased to invite you to a TAVIP Masterclass with Ed Rogers from Bristol Braille who will be talking about the development and launch of the Canute Scientific.

The inspiration behind the Canute Scientific has been to develop a machine which will empower blind people studying or working in the fields of Science, Technology, Engineering and Maths (STEM subjects).

Incorporating a 360-cell refreshable Braille display (9 × 40 cells) with a 13-inch synchronized visual monitor, the Canute Scientific enables blind and sighted users to collaborate equally on technical content.

As an evolution of their Canute Console, the Canute Scientific has a faster processor, new system board, thinner and lighter chassis and is built with improved production processes. It also has a lot more in the way of connectivity options, allowing people to work on various hardware projects and a suite of custom applications to work with various forms of data and schematics.

As with their other devices, this was built with feedback and testing by Braille readers.

Ed will talk about the design concept, the product details, and how it will be able to help people studying or working in technical career roles.

Whether or not you are in the market for a multi line braille display, do join us for what will be a really interesting discussion about the development of braille technology and it’s relevance in a wider range of subject areas.

Background to Bristol Braille

Whilst there have been efforts to develop more affordable single line displays, multiline Braille has typically been beyond the reach of most Braille readers, with devices costing into multiple thousands. This is despite the obvious advantages for productivity and greater context awareness that multiline Braille offers.

To try answering this, Ed rogers founded Bristol Braille with the mission to bring an affordable multi line Braille display to the market.

Since inception, Bristol Braille Technology has worked closely with Braille readers to test and develop their innovative solutions. They created the award winning world’s first affordable multiline Braille display, the Canute 360, releasing it in 2019. This followed many iterations and hands on feedback from Braille readers both in Bristol and beyond.

The Canute 360 display was followed by the Canute Console, a stand alone multi line Braille workstation. The console combined the 9 line Braille display with a high contrast visual HD monitor meaning both blind Braille readers and sighted colleagues could view the same information simultaneously.

Their machines are designed and built in the UK at their Bristol based workshop, which also hosts regular Braille Space events. These offer opportunities for people to try out the equipment and share ideas with likeminded folk.

Bristol Braille will also be taking the Canute Scientific on the road to various events this year, including Sight Village. Further details of events can be found at https://bristolbraille.org

As usual, the zoom details for the Masterclass are as follows:

If you are already logged in you can enter our ID 2222 397 064, or Connect to the TAVIP Zoom Room by clicking or tapping this link: https://zoom.us/j/2222397064 If you’d prefer, you can dial in on 0203 695 0088 and enter our meeting ID 2222 397 064. You don’t need to enter a participant ID.

item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: The Alternative Formats Service Manager will lead the Alternative Formats Team and Service and will strive to deliver an outstanding student experience, supporting a whole university approach to accessibility. The post-holder will provide operational management and expert knowledge regarding accessibility of teaching materials, texts and assessment materials. The role will involve managing a team of … Continue reading Job Vacancy: Alternative Formats Manager, Glasgow University, Deadline 28 July
item.content:encoded:
The Alternative Formats Service Manager will lead the Alternative Formats Team and Service and will strive to deliver an outstanding student experience, supporting a whole university approach to accessibility. The post-holder will provide operational management and expert knowledge regarding accessibility of teaching materials, texts and assessment materials.

The role will involve managing a team of Alternative Format Officers to deliver support to disabled students and ensure that the service provision of physical and digital accessible materials meet and exceed, where possible, statutory requirements. The post-holder will act as a leading advocate in the promotion of inclusivity and accessibility and ensure promotion and implementation across the University. They will also lead in the evaluation and, where appropriate, the deployment of innovative solutions to accessibility within teaching and learning.

Alternative Formats Manager

eyes On Success:

2626 Braille Blooms with New Tech from Perkins (Jul. 1, 2026)
Show Notes
Transcript

The Perkins Brailler is getting a digital upgrade that helps blind students transition into STEM careers and access online content. This budget-friendly tool translates mechanical typing into digital text. Hosts Nancy and Peter Torpey talk with Kim Charlson and Megan Gagne about how the Braille Bloom brings paper braille into the modern digital age.

You can download the episode from the link above or subscribe to the podcast wherever you get your podcasts if you don’t want to miss an episode.  You can also listen on your smart home device by saying “play the Eyes On Success podcast”.

Eyes On success is now also available on YouTube at:

www.youtube.com/@eyesonsuccess Enjoy and help promote the show by sharing with a friend!

Multi-line Braille has become an invaluable tool for me as an associate lecturer in computer science and a software developer. In this talk, I will give just a few examples of how multi-line Braille has been transformative in my work and home life and discuss my experience using the Canute Scientific Braille workstation and how open-source software and a close relationship with the Braillist community has made Bristol Braille’s products powerful and flexible tools for professionals working in STEM subjects.

item.content:encoded:
From the ACB National Convention:

HumanWare welcomes you to join Joel, Roger and Kevin as they present on  “What’s New with HumanWare”. More specifically, how HumanWare “redefines” what a BrailleNote is with the new BrailleNote Evolve. The exciting Evolve is a full Windows 11 PC coming to you in a compact form factor with 32 cells of Braille. The Evolve delivers a seamless braille first experience powered by NVDA and Keysoft. The HumanWare team will also discuss the current state of Victor Stream, Ray Ban Meta glasses and some of our popular low vision tools.

Presenters:

  • Joel Zimba, Blindness Products Specialist
  • Kevin Hughes, Regional Sales Manager

Roger Steinberg, Product Manager Low Vision Products

item.title: Hands On With Braille: the Whys and Wherefores of Visiting an Exhibition, Tuesday at 7:30 PM
item.dc:creator: Matthew Horspool
item.description: “So many products, so little time!” We hear this a lot when it comes to blindness exhibitions and, with the summer shows just around the corner, we thought we’d take some time to discuss what you can do to make the most of having such a vast selection of braille products on display in one … Continue reading Hands On With Braille: the Whys and Wherefores of Visiting an Exhibition, Tuesday at 7:30 PM
item.content:encoded:
“So many products, so little time!”

We hear this a lot when it comes to blindness exhibitions and, with the summer shows just around the corner, we thought we’d take some time to discuss what you can do to make the most of having such a vast selection of braille products on display in one place.

  • Which braille products should I prioritise?
  • How can I find them?
  • What questions should I ask?
  • How can I decide which one will best meet my needs?

Our panel of experts will consider all of these questions and offer their strategies for making sense of the exhibition hall. Along the way, we’ll also talk about tips for navigating in noisy and crowded spaces, travel, accommodation, budget and much more.

Register for Hands On With Braille
